weeks.title: Salt and Light in the World
weeks.theme: A disciple’s social life is the mission frontline: salt must flavor, light must be seen, and the glory goes to the Father.
group: Read Matthew 5:13-16. What does salt do, what does light do, and why does Jesus say “You are” rather than “You must become”?
In your workplace, neighborhood, or group chats, are you more like “salt that has lost its flavor” or “a lamp under a basket”?
What is one “flavorful” good deed you could do this week for your neighborhood or community?
weeks.sunday: With your family or small group, take a half-hour walk around your neighborhood. As you walk, pray quietly for the shops, schools, building office, and neighbors you pass, asking God to give this city peace. Then choose one small thing to do—thank the building manager, pick up litter along the street, or stop by a quiet little shop and greet the owner sincerely. When you get home, thank God for placing you here.

lessons.title: You Are Salt, You Are Light
lessons.hear:
At the start of the Sermon on the Mount, right after the Beatitudes, Jesus said two astonishing things to a crowd of fishermen, farmers, and tax collectors: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13). “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14). Notice that he didn’t say, “Try hard to become salt and light.” He said, “You are.” This is identity, not performance. We have already been placed in the world, like salt rubbed into meat or a lamp set in a house. The question isn’t whether to become salt and light but whether we will lose our flavor or be covered up.

In the ancient world salt had two uses: preserving and flavoring. To do its work it has to make contact and be worked in; salt left in the jar is useless no matter how salty it is. So a Christian’s social life isn’t optional leisure—it is the mission frontline. Team dinners, parents’ group chats, the homeowners’ association, the gym, class reunions: these are all places where salt must work its way in. But salt can also lose its flavor. When we join in the mockery in a group chat or the gossip at dinner, we become no different from everyone around us.

The danger for light is the opposite: not blending in but hiding. “Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand” (Matthew 5:15). Some Christians shine only inside the church and switch off the moment they leave. Their friends are all believers, and their weekday lives barely intersect with the world. Such a lamp is safe, but it doesn’t light anyone’s way.

Jesus also explains the purpose of shining: “that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). Light isn’t meant to make people look at the lamp but to help them see the road—and see the Father. This is the balance of salt and light: go deep into everyday life without losing your flavor; be seen, yet give the glory to God.
lessons.light: Our identity as salt and light comes from the Lord who said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). Keep the focus on Jesus, not on ourselves: we aren’t suns that shine on our own but moons that reflect him. Letting Jesus receive all the glory is the only purpose of shining—and it is where building God’s system begins.
think: In Matthew 5:13-16, what can go wrong with salt, and what can go wrong with light?
Is my social life more like salt that has “lost its flavor” or a lamp “under a basket”?
In which community today can I let people taste a slightly different “flavor”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for calling me the salt of the earth and the light of the world. This is the identity you gave me, not something I earned. Forgive me for sometimes drifting with the crowd and losing my flavor, and sometimes hiding under a basket. Today, send me into the crowd so that people taste your grace and see the Father’s glory—not me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, list three non-church communities you are part of every week (work, neighborhood, group chats, and so on). Pray one sentence for each, asking the Lord to make you salt and light there.
lessons.quick: Salt must flavor, light must be seen—and the glory goes to the Father.
text: “You are the salt of the earth, but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will it be salted? It is then good for nothing, but to be cast out and trodden under the feet of men.
“You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.
Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.
Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

lessons.title: The One Who Doesn’t Complain
lessons.hear:
A woman working at a trading company had an after-hours “venting chat” with her office colleagues. Every evening they took turns complaining about managers, clients, and company policy, getting more worked up as they went. At first she chimed in too, but she noticed that afterward she felt even worse, and at home she had less patience with her children. She thought, “I’m not sharing the gospel. What kind of witness can a Christian possibly have in a chat like this?”

This is a common old mindset: witnessing means making arguments, handing out gospel tracts, or taking a stand on controversial issues; everyday socializing is just socializing and has nothing to do with witness. But Paul’s teaching to the Philippians starts in the most ordinary place: “Do all things without complaining and arguing, that you may become blameless and harmless, children of God without defect in the middle of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you are seen as lights in the world” (Philippians 2:14-15).

It turns out that not complaining is a way of shining. In a group used to grumbling, someone who doesn’t join in—and who can still see the good in others—is like a star in the night sky. She doesn’t need to raise her voice, yet she stands out. God’s view is that witness doesn’t only happen in the pulpit; it happens even more in the break room, the group chat, and around the dinner table.

She didn’t leave the chat, and she didn’t lecture anyone. She simply stopped joining in the complaints, and now and then she would post, “Thanks to my coworker next door for taking that difficult call for me today.” Sometimes she said, “The boss’s decision today was exhausting, but things with the client really do seem to be going more smoothly.” A few months later, a colleague asked her privately, “How come you never seem to get worn down enough to complain?” That evening, in a café, she found herself talking naturally for the first time about her morning prayers.
lessons.light: Complaining is the voice of the self-centered life: my hard work, my unfair treatment. The selfless don’t pretend there are no difficulties; they bring their difficulties to God and bring their thanks to people. Lead with the heart and you find joy; lead with the head and you find worry. A heart filled with the Holy Spirit will naturally shine in a crooked generation.
think: In Philippians 2:14-16, how is “without complaining” connected to being “seen as lights in the world”?
In which group chat or setting am I most likely to join in the complaining?
Can I say one word of thanks or appreciation there today?
lessons.speak: Father, forgive me for treating complaining as conversation and sighing along with the world. Cleanse my mouth and make me blameless and harmless in a crooked and perverse generation. In group chats, break rooms, and around the table, let a word of thanks and an attitude free of complaint make me a light in the world. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in a chat or setting where complaining is common, don’t join in. Instead, specifically thank or appreciate a coworker, family member, or neighbor for something they did well.
lessons.quick: Not complaining where everyone complains—that is shining.
text: Do all things without complaining and arguing,
that you may become blameless and harmless, children of God without defect in the middle of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you are seen as lights in the world,
holding up the word of life, that I may have something to boast in the day of Christ that I didn’t run in vain nor labor in vain.

lessons.title: Seek the Peace of the City
lessons.hear:
The Jews carried off to Babylon probably wanted two things most: to dream of going home every day, and to have as little to do with the Babylonians as possible. But through Jeremiah God wrote to them: “Build houses and dwell in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit” (Jeremiah 29:5). And again: “Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace you will have peace” (Jeremiah 29:7).

This letter fits Chinese Christians today especially well. Some of us are new immigrants, some are international students, some have moved from the countryside to a big city, and some have moved in with their adult children after retirement. It is easy to feel that this isn’t really my place—I’m only passing through—and to keep our circle of friends limited to people from the same hometown, language, or church. But God says: put down roots here, and be a blessing here. Salt can’t stay in its own jar.

For today’s practice, choose one action that lets the salt work its way in. First, get to know people: learn the names of your building manager, the owner of the breakfast shop you visit, and your next-door neighbor, and greet them by name next time. Second, get involved: if your community has a street cleanup, a charity sale, elder care, or school volunteering, sign up once. Third, intercede: pray specifically for your city, district, or school—for its safety, education, and needs. None of these is a big thing, but each one is a grain of salt sprinkled into the city.

Be wise as well. As you get involved in the community, if you’re invited to join an investment, lend money, or meet someone alone late at night, know how to decline politely. Salt must work its way in, but it doesn’t have to give up its boundaries. When you begin to pray for a place, you’ll find you are no longer just someone who lives there—you are someone God has sent there.
lessons.light: Seeking the peace of the city is the Lord’s Prayer brought down to earth: your kingdom come, on the very street where I live. Our one purpose is to build God’s system, and that doesn’t start with a grand plan; it starts with calling a neighbor by name. Change begins with me—at my own front door.
think: In Jeremiah 29:4-7, what does God tell the exiles to do in a foreign land?
Do I treat the place where I live now as merely a temporary “Babylon”?
Whose name will I learn today, or for which place will I pray specifically?
lessons.speak: Father, you placed me in this city, this neighborhood, this building. Forgive me for caring only about my own small circle and treating this place like a temporary inn. Help me put down roots here and seek the peace of this city, so that your kingdom comes to the street right outside my door. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, ask the name of someone you see often but don’t know by name (a building manager, shopkeeper, or neighbor). Write it down, greet them by name next time you meet, and pray for them.
lessons.quick: Seek the peace of the city, because God has sent you there.
text: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says to all the captives whom I have caused to be carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon:
“Build houses and dwell in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit.
Take wives and father sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters. Multiply there, and don’t be diminished.
Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace you will have peace.”

lessons.title: A Warning Taken as a Joke
lessons.hear:
Lot lived in Sodom for many years. At first he “moved his tent as far as Sodom” (Genesis 13:12); later, “Lot sat in the gate of Sodom” (Genesis 19:1), a man of standing with connections, and his daughters were engaged to local men. Scripture calls him a “righteous man” who “was tormented in his righteous soul from day to day with seeing and hearing lawless deeds” (2 Peter 2:8). Yet when judgment drew near and the angels told him to take his family and leave, a heartbreaking scene unfolded: “Lot went out, and spoke to his sons-in-law… and said, ‘Get up! Get out of this place, for the LORD will destroy the city!’ But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be joking” (Genesis 19:14).

Why were the most important words he ever spoke taken as a joke? Perhaps because Lot’s life was no longer very different from the city’s. He grieved inside, but no one could see it from the outside. Jesus said, “if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will it be salted?” (Matthew 5:13). Losing flavor doesn’t necessarily mean committing some great evil. It means being assimilated little by little, until nothing we say carries any weight.

Let Lot be a mirror for you. If tomorrow I spoke seriously about my faith at work or at a family dinner, would people take me seriously, or think I was joking? Do I often laugh along at snide jokes, join in the complaining, or cut small corners? Does my light shine only on Sunday and get dimmed down to its lowest setting on Monday?

The text goes on: “But he lingered” (Genesis 19:16). Even Lot himself was reluctant to leave. Yet grace came right after: “the men grabbed his hand, his wife’s hand, and his two daughters’ hands, the LORD being merciful to him; and they took him out” (Genesis 19:16). God didn’t give up on this flavorless salt; he took him by the hand himself.

The way to adjust isn’t to withdraw from people and hide in the church. It is to let the flavor come back—to live differently from those around you in one concrete matter. Stop telling one kind of joke you usually laugh along with, keep one small promise, be honest in one small thing. When your life has flavor again, your words will carry weight.
lessons.light: Salt losing its flavor is the assimilation of the self-centered life: afraid of not fitting in or being laughed at, we let our surroundings define us bit by bit. The selfless don’t need to be odd or showy, yet because they let Jesus reign, they naturally carry a different flavor. God’s mercy took Lot by the hand, and it takes ours too. Change begins with me: when my life has flavor first, my relationships and witness gain weight.
think: In Genesis 19:12-16, how did Lot’s sons-in-law react to his warning, and why?
Would my friends take my faith seriously, or treat it as a joke?
In what specific small matter will I let my “flavor” come back today?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that sometimes I am like Lot, assimilated little by little by my surroundings until my words lose their weight. Thank you for your mercy—you still take me by the hand. Restore the flavor to my life, so that at work, in group chats, and in my extended family I live like you, and people see my good works and give glory to you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose one joke, complaint, or small shortcut you usually go along with, and stop it in one specific situation. Tonight, look back on the day and thank God for his help.
lessons.quick: When our lives lose their flavor, our words are taken as a joke.
text: The men said to Lot, “Do you have anybody else here? Sons-in-law, your sons, your daughters, and whomever you have in the city, bring them out of the place:
for we will destroy this place, because the outcry against them has grown so great before the LORD that the LORD has sent us to destroy it.”

Lot went out, and spoke to his sons-in-law, who were pledged to marry his daughters, and said, “Get up! Get out of this place, for the LORD will destroy the city!” But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be joking.
When the morning came, then the angels hurried Lot, saying, “Get up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be consumed in the iniquity of the city.”
But he lingered; and the men grabbed his hand, his wife’s hand, and his two daughters’ hands, the LORD being merciful to him; and they took him out, and set him outside of the city.

lessons.title: Your Light Will Break Out as the Morning
lessons.hear:
The people of Isaiah’s day were zealous about religious activity—fasting, praying, keeping the feasts—yet they complained that God didn’t notice. God answered: the fast I have chosen is “to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house” (Isaiah 58:7). Then comes a beautiful promise: “Then your light will break out as the morning” (Isaiah 58:8).

Notice that this light isn’t switched on by effort; it breaks out naturally as we love people. Like morning light, it needs no advertising—the day simply dawns. God goes on: “If you take away from among you the yoke, finger pointing, and speaking wickedly” (Isaiah 58:9), then “your obscurity will be as the noonday” (Isaiah 58:10). Laying down blame and stopping harsh words is itself the beginning of letting the light in.

This week we have seen that we are salt and light—this is our identity. Not complaining where everyone complains is shining. Seeking the peace of the city where we live lets the salt work its way in. And in Lot we saw that salt that has lost its flavor speaks without weight. Now repeat it: each day before you head out, remind yourself with one sentence: “Lord, make me salt and light today at my workplace, in my neighborhood, at my school.”

Then multiply it. A single grain of salt rarely does much on its own, and light grows brighter the more of it there is. Invite a friend or your small group to do one small act of blessing for your community together: visit an elderly neighbor who lives alone, put together a care package for a struggling family nearby, or volunteer once at a school or community center. Pray together before you go and give thanks together afterward. When a group of people shines together, that corner of the world truly lights up.
lessons.light: The last step on the Way of Service is “God”: all glory to God. Isaiah 58 reminds us that true godliness can be seen and touched—a bowl of rice, an open home. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: when our lives are renewed, ministry rises naturally like the morning light.
think: In Isaiah 58:6-10, what does the “fast” that God values look like?
Does my faith mostly stay inside church gatherings, rarely reaching into people’s real needs?
Whom will I invite to join me in one small act of blessing for our community?
lessons.speak: Father, take away my pointing finger and my harsh tongue, and turn my heart in compassion toward those who are suffering. Let my light break out not through self-promotion but naturally, like the morning. Lead me and my brothers and sisters into our community together, so that people see your glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite a friend or small group member to set a time to do one act of blessing for your community together (visiting an elderly neighbor who lives alone, delivering supplies, or volunteering). Pray together before you go.
lessons.quick: Light isn’t forced out; it breaks out naturally as we love.
text: “Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to release the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and that you break every yoke?

Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?
Then your light will break out as the morning, and your healing will appear quickly; then your righteousness shall go before you, and the LORD’s glory will be your rear guard.
Then you will call, and the LORD will answer. You will cry for help, and he will say, ‘Here I am.’ “If you take away from among you the yoke, finger pointing, and speaking wickedly;
and if you pour out your soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul, then your light will rise in darkness, and your obscurity will be as the noonday;

weeks.title: Gospel Friendship
weeks.theme: Friendship is not a tool for evangelism—the gospel is the truest love within a friendship; walk in wisdom and let your speech be gracious.
group: Read Colossians 4:2-6. Before Paul talks about how to treat “those who are outside,” what does he mention first, and why?
Have you ever avoided mentioning your faith for fear of rejection or of sounding like a salesperson, or made someone feel like a target?
This week, which friend outside the church are you willing to pray for and invite to do something relaxed together?
weeks.sunday: Invite a friend or neighbor from outside the church to your home for a simple home-cooked meal, or go hiking or out for afternoon tea together. Pray for them beforehand, asking God to open a door for conversation. While you’re together, ask more about their life and their story, and don’t rush to make a point. If they ask about your faith, share naturally. Afterward, thank God for the friendship itself, whether or not the gospel came up.

lessons.title: Walk in Wisdom Toward Outsiders
lessons.hear:
When Paul wrote Colossians, he was in chains in prison. He didn’t ask the church to pray for his release; he asked them to pray “that God may open to us a door for the word” (Colossians 4:3). Then he turned his gaze to every believer’s daily life: “Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one” (Colossians 4:5-6).

These few verses sketch a map of gospel friendship. The first stop is prayer: “Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving” (Colossians 4:2). God opens the door; we don’t pry it open. So we don’t need to be anxious or pushy. The second stop is wisdom: “those who are outside” aren’t enemies or sales targets; they are people God loves and whom we genuinely want to know. Wisdom means understanding boundaries, timing, and the other person’s situation.

The third stop is redeeming the time. This doesn’t mean turning every coffee into an evangelistic rally; it means not letting a friendship stay on the surface. Many people are coworkers, neighbors, or classmates for ten years and still know nothing about each other’s lives. The fourth stop is our speech: “with grace, seasoned with salt.” Salt gives food its flavor, but you can’t use too much. Our words should carry grace and warmth without lecturing or force-feeding.

The last phrase is beautiful: “that you may know how you ought to answer each one.” Each one—not everyone at once. Gospel friendship has no one-size-fits-all script, because every person’s story is different. Some need to be heard, some need help, and some come with honest questions. Our task is to get to know the one person in front of us and then follow the Holy Spirit’s guidance to say what fits their need.
lessons.light: Gospel friendship rests on this: relationships matter more than things—and more than results. Self-centered evangelism wants to prove its own spiritual fruitfulness; selfless gospel friendship simply wants a friend to meet Jesus, without even needing to keep the credit. The Holy Spirit is my guide: when the door opens and what to say are both up to him.
think: What elements of gospel friendship does Paul mention in Colossians 4:2-6?
Do my relationships with friends outside the church mostly stay on the surface?
For which friend can I pray today, “Lord, open a door”?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for seeking me through friendship and loving me while I was still an outsider. Open doors for the word among my friends, coworkers, and neighbors. Help me redeem the time, walk in wisdom, and let my speech always be with grace, so that I know how to answer each one. Keep me from treating people as targets; let me simply love them. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the name of a friend outside the church and pray for them: “Lord, open a door.” Then send them a message of sincere interest in how they’re doing—it’s fine not to mention faith at all.
lessons.quick: God opens the door; I just keep praying and speak with grace.
text: Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving,
praying together for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds,
that I may reveal it as I ought to speak.
Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time.
Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.

lessons.title: A Conversation That Began with Water
lessons.hear:
A young woman went to New Zealand on a working holiday and shared a house with three young people from different countries. Before she left, her church had trained her and she had memorized a gospel outline, determined to seize every opportunity. On her third day in the house, she presented sin and salvation over dinner. Her housemates listened politely—and afterward began timing their meals so they wouldn’t overlap with hers. She was discouraged: “Am I not supposed to share the gospel?”

Behind this lies a common old mindset: evangelism means getting through a set of content, the sooner the better, and friendship is just a tool for evangelism. God’s perspective is clearest in Jesus’ conversation at the well. He didn’t begin with a sermon but with a request: “Give me a drink” (John 4:7). A Jewish man asking a Samaritan woman for water crossed three walls at once—ethnicity, gender, and reputation. He made himself the one in need and gave her dignity.

Then Jesus moved from the water in front of them to living water: “whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again” (John 4:14). He didn’t force a change of subject; he found, within her everyday life, a door that opened onto eternity. He also listened and responded to her questions, letting her discover step by step what she was really thirsty for.

Later, that young woman changed her approach. She asked her housemates to teach her their home cooking and made Taiwanese braised pork rice for everyone in return. When one of them went through a breakup, she went on walks with her late into the evening (nearby, with other housemates along). Six months later, a housemate asked, “What do you do in your room every morning?” She said, “I pray—and I pray for all of you.” The housemate was quiet for a moment, then said, “Could you pray for my mom too? She’s sick.” In that moment she understood: the gospel isn’t stuffed into a friendship; it flows naturally out of one.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he crossed the wall first, became the one who needed help first, and listened first. Self-centered evangelism only cares about getting through my content; selfless gospel friendship sees the other person’s thirst. Friendship has value in itself—even if the other person hasn’t yet come to faith, that love is never wasted.
think: In John 4:7-15, how does Jesus open and guide this conversation?
Have I ever treated friendship as a tool, or the gospel as content I must get through?
How could I let a friend do me a small favor, so that our relationship is more mutual?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, at the well you asked an outcast woman for water and crossed every wall. Forgive me for sometimes treating people as targets and rushing to say what I want to say. Help me see my friends’ thirst first—to listen first and walk alongside them first—so that your living water flows naturally out of real friendship. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, ask a friend outside the church for advice on something they’re good at (cooking, repairs, work, or travel). Listen sincerely and thank them, so the friendship becomes more natural and more mutual.
lessons.quick: The gospel isn’t stuffed into a friendship; it flows out of one.
text: A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”
For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.
The Samaritan woman therefore said to him, “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”
The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. So where do you get that living water?
Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his children and his livestock?”
Jesus answered her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again,
but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.”
The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I don’t get thirsty, neither come all the way here to draw.”

lessons.title: Always Ready to Give an Answer
lessons.hear:
Peter wrote to Christians who were misunderstood and pushed to the margins of their society. He didn’t teach them debating techniques. Instead he said: “But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear” (1 Peter 3:15).

Notice the order. First, “sanctify the Lord God in your hearts”: gospel friendship doesn’t start with our mouths but with letting Jesus reign in our hearts. Second, “everyone who asks you”: gospel friendship is usually a response, not an ambush. When our lives carry hope and peace, people naturally become curious. Third, “always be ready”: when someone asks, don’t stammer—and don’t talk for an hour straight either. Fourth, “with humility and fear”: don’t argue, don’t dismiss their questions, and respect their freedom to choose.

Today’s practice is to prepare your “three-minute story.” Write it in three parts: what my life was like (or what I was searching for) before I knew Jesus; how I met him; and how he is changing my life and relationships now. Use everyday language, not church jargon. Tell your real experience, including the areas where you are still learning. An honest story moves people more than a perfect theory.

Then pray for the people around you. In the app’s Five Names feature, you can write down five friends from outside the church and pray for them every day. Remember, this isn’t a to-do list; it’s a prayer list of love. They aren’t your targets; they are your friends. Maybe they’ll ask a year from now; maybe they’ll never ask. Either way, your prayers and your friendship are in God’s hands.
lessons.light: To “sanctify the Lord God in your hearts” is to let Jesus reign. Gospel friendship flows from there, not from technique. The selfless don’t need to win the debate; they simply bear honest witness. Lean on the Holy Spirit with your heart rather than on yourself with your head—the Spirit will remind you of the right words at the right time.
think: In 1 Peter 3:15-16, what kind of heart and attitude should we have when we answer others?
If someone asked me today, “Why do you believe in Jesus?” could I answer clearly and with humility?
In my three-minute story, which turning point best shows how Jesus has changed me?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I want to sanctify you in my heart and let you reign in my life. Make my life so full of hope that people become curious, and when they ask, help me always be ready to answer with humility and fear. I place my five friends in your hands—not as targets, but as people you love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write your three-minute faith story in three parts. Then open the app’s Five Names, write down five friends outside the church, and pray one sentence for each.
lessons.quick: When Christ is Lord in our hearts, our answers can be humble and gentle.
text: Now who will harm you if you become imitators of that which is good?
But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed. “Don’t fear what they fear, neither be troubled.”
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear,
having a good conscience. Thus, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ.
For it is better, if it is God’s will, that you suffer for doing what is right than for doing evil.

lessons.title: The Disciples Saw Only Lunch
lessons.hear:
While Jesus was talking with the Samaritan woman, the disciples had gone into town to buy food. When they came back, “They marveled that he was speaking with a woman” (John 4:27). They had questions but didn’t dare ask. What they saw was “someone he shouldn’t be talking to,” not a thirsty soul. Then they cared about just one thing: “Rabbi, eat” (John 4:31).

At that same noon hour, the woman left her water jar and ran into town calling out to people—while the disciples were thinking about lunch. They had just come from that same town and passed the same Samaritans, probably wanting only to finish their shopping and get out quickly. Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work,” and, “lift up your eyes and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already” (John 4:34-35).

Today, let the disciples be a mirror for you. First, do I see only tasks and not people? The coworkers, store clerks, and delivery drivers I pass every day may be mere “functions” to me rather than people with stories. Second, do I have invisible walls? Do I privately think certain people “could never believe” or “aren’t our kind of people”? Third, has my circle of friends shrunk to Christians only, so that I don’t have a single friend outside the church with whom I can really talk?

We should also review a distortion in the other direction: do I treat people as targets? Warm only when I want to share the gospel, then cool once they show no interest? That kind of “friendship” also fails to see the person. The adjustment is in Jesus’ words: “lift up your eyes.” Lift your head out of your own busyness and assumptions, and see the person in front of you. They are loved by God, and whether or not they believe, they deserve to be treated with sincerity.
lessons.light: Relationships matter more than things; people matter more than tasks. The disciples’ eyes stayed on the lunch in front of them; Jesus’ eyes were on heaven’s harvest. Change your perspective and you change your mindset. The “2” in the 920 isn’t only people in church; it is also everyone who brushes past me each day, waiting to be seen.
think: In John 4:27-35, what did the disciples see, and what did Jesus see?
Among the people I pass each day, whom do I treat as a “function” rather than a person?
How will I “lift up my eyes” today and truly see someone?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, forgive me for so often seeing only my lunch and my schedule and not the people around me—and forgive me for sometimes treating people as targets, warm one moment and cool the next. Open my eyes so that I lift them up and see the people you love, and treat them sincerely whether they respond or not. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, stop for someone you see often but rarely talk with (a store clerk, delivery driver, cleaner, or coworker). Call them by name or greet them sincerely, and ask one more question about how they’re doing.
lessons.quick: Lift up your eyes: see the person first, and then you’ll see the harvest.
text: Just then, his disciples came. They marveled that he was speaking with a woman; yet no one said, “What are you looking for?” or, “Why do you speak with her?”
So the woman left her water pot, went away into the city, and said to the people,
“Come, see a man who told me everything that I have done. Can this be the Christ?”
They went out of the city, and were coming to him.
In the meanwhile, the disciples urged him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.”
But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you don’t know about.”
The disciples therefore said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?”
Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.
Don’t you say, ‘There are yet four months until the harvest’? Behold, I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already.

lessons.title: Inviting Friends: Come and See
lessons.hear:
After Andrew met Jesus, the first thing he did was simple: “He first found his own brother, Simon… He brought him to Jesus” (John 1:41-42). No big evangelistic rally—just one brother bringing another to meet someone. And the Simon he brought became the apostle Peter.

Philip’s story is even more interesting. He excitedly told his friend Nathanael, who poured cold water on it: “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?” Philip didn’t argue or get upset. He simply said, “Come and see” (John 1:46). He didn’t need to answer every question; he only needed to bring his friend to the Lord who could.

This week we have learned that gospel friendship begins with prayer, asking God to open a door. Like Jesus at the well, real conversations begin with a drink of water or a meal. We are always ready to give an answer, with humility. And we lift up our eyes to see the people around us, never treating them as targets. Now repeat it: pray one sentence each day for the friends on your prayer list, and watch for whether God is opening a door.

Then multiply it. Gospel friendship is never a solo effort. Paul says, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). You can invite a friend to a relaxed small group meal, a concert, or a talk on everyday life, so they can see a group of Christians who genuinely love one another. You can also pray with your small group for each other’s friends. You don’t have to carry your friend’s whole faith journey alone. Like Philip, you only need to say gently at the right moment, “Come and see.” Whether or not they come, you don’t withdraw your friendship.
lessons.light: Spiritual companions in the 235 are also co-workers in gospel friendship: one plants, another waters, and the glory goes to God who gives the growth. The selfless don’t compete to be “the one who led them to Christ”; they simply serve faithfully as a bridge. Let Jesus receive all the glory.
think: In John 1:40-46, how did Andrew and Philip bring people to Jesus?
When a friend is skeptical, do I rush to argue, or can I simply say, “Come and see”?
Which friend can I invite to a relaxed gathering where they can see a real Christian community?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for teaching me through Andrew and Philip the simplest way to bring people to you. I don’t need to answer every question; I only need to invite my friends to “come and see.” Make our small group a community of genuine love, so that friends who come see you. And whether or not they respond, help me never withdraw my friendship. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, ask your small group to pray for one friend on your prayer list (without revealing anything private about them), and invite that friend to a relaxed meal or activity.
lessons.quick: You don’t need to answer every question—just say, “Come and see.”
text: One of the two who heard John and followed him was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother.
He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, “We have found the Messiah!” (which is, being interpreted, Christ).
He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas” (which is by interpretation, Peter).
On the next day, he was determined to go out into Galilee, and he found Philip. Jesus said to him, “Follow me.”
Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.
Philip found Nathanael, and said to him, “We have found him of whom Moses in the law and also the prophets, wrote: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”
Nathanael said to him, “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”

weeks.keyText: Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time.

weeks.title: The Witness of Good Works
weeks.theme: The world may not read the Bible, but it reads our lives every day—good character is the loudest witness.
group: Read 1 Peter 2:11-12. When Christians are slandered, what does Peter tell us to respond with?
At work, in your neighborhood, or online, have your words and actions ever shown people a “church self” and a different “outside self”?
This week, in what small matter will you let people see Christ through honesty or gentleness?
weeks.sunday: As a family, do a “return and thank” project. Find things you borrowed and never gave back (a book, an umbrella, a food container) and return them with a little thank-you card. Or write a card to someone who regularly serves you, such as a building manager, teacher, or cleaner. Pray together before you go, asking the Lord to let them feel loved; afterward, thank God together for the chance to be a small witness.

lessons.title: Good Behavior Among the Nations
lessons.hear:
Peter was writing to Christians scattered across Asia Minor. Because they refused to worship idols and stayed away from certain kinds of revelry, their neighbors pointed fingers at them and even called them strange or wicked. Peter didn’t tell them to protest in the streets, nor did he tell them to hide their faith. Instead he said they should be “having good behavior among the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good works and glorify God in the day of visitation” (1 Peter 2:12).

The “good works” here carry the sense of goodness that is beautiful and visible. These aren’t good deeds done in secret but a life lived in front of others that holds up under observation. The world may not read the Bible, but it reads us every day: how we treat a restaurant server, how we reply to an offensive message in a group chat, how we file expense reports, whether we keep our time and our word. We are the book in their hands.

Peter also reminds us that such a life begins with two identities. First, we are “foreigners and pilgrims” (1 Peter 2:11): our home is in heaven, so we don’t need to grab for fame and gain the way the world does. Second, we live “as bondservants of God” (1 Peter 2:16): we are free, yet we don’t use our freedom as a cover. From this flows a balanced attitude toward society: “Honor all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17). Honoring all people includes those with different views and different faiths.

As for submitting to every human institution, this isn’t blind obedience. If an institution requires us to disobey God, the apostles also said, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). But in the vast majority of everyday life, a Christian’s best response isn’t to shout the loudest but to live the most beautifully.
lessons.light: Our identity as pilgrims shifts our perspective from earth to heaven: we don’t need to win the moment, but we do need to live for eternity. Let Jesus receive all the glory—the purpose of good works isn’t for people to praise me but for them to “glorify God.” This is the quietest and yet most powerful way to build God’s system.
think: In 1 Peter 2:11-17, what concrete guidance does Peter give to “foreigners and pilgrims”?
If someone knew Christians only through my life, what impression would they get?
How can I “honor” someone today whose views or faith differ from mine?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for making me a citizen of heaven and a pilgrim on earth. Help me keep good behavior among the nations—to live out good works at work, in my neighborhood, and online, to honor all people, and never to use my freedom as a cloak for wickedness. May people see not me, but your glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, be especially courteous to someone who serves you (a store clerk, driver, customer service agent, or delivery driver). Thank them sincerely and use their name or title, so they feel respected.
lessons.quick: The world may not read the Bible, but it reads our lives every day.
text: Beloved, I beg you as foreigners and pilgrims to abstain from fleshly lusts which war against the soul,
having good behavior among the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good works and glorify God in the day of visitation.
Therefore subject yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake: whether to the king, as supreme,
or to governors, as sent by him for vengeance on evildoers and for praise to those who do well.
For this is the will of God, that by well-doing you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish men.
Live as free people, yet not using your freedom for a cloak of wickedness, but as bondservants of God.
Honor all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king.

lessons.title: No Fault to Be Found
lessons.hear:
Soon after a man took a purchasing job at a construction company, he discovered that everyone in his department accepted “holiday gifts” from suppliers—and some took cash kickbacks. A coworker patted him on the shoulder and said, “Everyone does it. If you don’t take it, people will think you’re holier-than-thou, and you’ll have a hard time here.” He wrestled inside: if he refused, would he be shut out? Would people say he was putting on airs?

Behind this is a very common old mindset: to survive in society you need some gray areas; witness is for Sunday, and work is something else. God’s perspective can be seen in Daniel. He served as a high official in a pagan empire, and his jealous colleagues schemed to find something wrong with him. But “they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him” (Daniel 6:4). In the end they could only say they would have to find something against him concerning the law of his God (see Daniel 6:5).

Think how high a compliment that is: even your enemies admit that your only “problem” is that you love your God too much. Daniel didn’t earn respect through eloquence but through years and years of faithfulness in small things. “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). The witness of good works isn’t a speech; it is a life that can stand up to an audit.

The man didn’t criticize anyone in meetings. He simply declined the suppliers’ gifts privately and courteously, and he reported his expenses honestly. At first, some people did say he was hard to get along with. Two years later, an internal audit found problems in the department, and his manager deliberately handed him an important project, saying, “I know you’re not someone who cuts corners.” That evening a coworker asked him privately, “Are all you Christians like this?” He smiled and said, “We’re all learning—because that’s how our Lord treats us.”
lessons.light: The temptation of the gray area is the survival rule of the self-centered life: protect yourself first and talk about principles later. The selfless leave the outcome to God, so they can be faithful in small things. To let Jesus reign means that even receipts, expense reports, and time sheets are under his lordship.
think: In Daniel 6:1-5, why couldn’t Daniel’s colleagues find anything against him?
In which “everyone does it” small matters might I already have compromised?
In what small matter will I choose to be faithful like Daniel today?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that I often talk myself into things with “everyone does it.” Give me Daniel’s resolve to be faithful in the smallest things and honest where no one is watching. Even if I am misunderstood or shut out, keep me from criticizing others or acting superior; let me simply love you, so that people see you in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, examine one small matter where you may have compromised (expense claims, reasons for taking leave, borrowing company property, online returns). Correct it honestly right away, and pray about it.
lessons.quick: The witness of good works is a life that can stand up to an audit.
text: It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom one hundred twenty local governors, who should be throughout the whole kingdom;
and over them three presidents, of whom Daniel was one, that these local governors might give account to them, and that the king should suffer no loss.
Then this Daniel was distinguished above the presidents and the local governors, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm.

Then the presidents and the local governors sought to find occasion against Daniel as touching the kingdom; but they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him.
Then these men said, “We won’t find any occasion against this Daniel, unless we find it against him concerning the law of his God.”

lessons.title: Gentle Toward All
lessons.hear:
Paul instructed Titus to remind the Christians on Crete “to speak evil of no one, not to be contentious, to be gentle, showing all humility toward all men” (Titus 3:2). In those days Cretans were known for being quarrelsome and dishonest. In that kind of environment, gentleness was the most striking witness of all.

We, too, live in a hot-tempered society: horns blaring in traffic, people cutting in line, homeowners’ association meetings that turn into shouting matches, comment sections full of insults. In these public places, a Christian’s witness doesn’t lie in delivering grand truths but in how we react. Someone who doesn’t curse when another driver steals their parking space, someone at the association meeting who refuses to attack people personally and is willing to hear opposing views—they make people more curious than any tract ever could.

Paul also tells us where the strength for gentleness comes from: “For we were also once foolish, disobedient, deceived… living in malice and envy” (Titus 3:3). We are not better than others; we are people who have received mercy. “not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us” (Titus 3:5). When we remember how much grace we have received, we stop looking down on the world from a superior height, and gentleness comes naturally.

For today’s practice, choose one public setting and deliberately live out gentleness. Let another car in while you’re driving. When you see a provocative comment online, don’t fire back. In an association meeting, a parents’ meeting, or a work meeting, say “I understand your concern” before giving your view. When a store clerk is rude, offer a little extra understanding. Gentleness isn’t weakness, and it isn’t having no convictions; it is having strength and choosing not to wound.
lessons.light: Gentleness is a fruit of the Spirit—what the “9” of the 920 looks like in public. Pride provokes pride, as we see everywhere online and in meetings; humility inspires humility, and one gentle word can cool an entire room. Remembering that we are people who have received mercy brings us back to our proper place.
think: In Titus 3:1-7, what attitudes for living in society does Paul set out?
In which public setting am I most likely to lose my gentleness?
Where can I deliberately “yield once” today?
lessons.speak: Father, I too was once foolish and disobedient, and you saved me according to your mercy. Help me remember this grace, so that in public I speak evil of no one, am not contentious, and am gentle toward all. When I am offended, Holy Spirit, remind me that gentleness isn’t weakness; it is having strength and choosing not to wound. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in one public setting (driving, waiting in line, a meeting, or online comments), deliberately respond with gentleness once: let someone go first, don’t fire back, or begin with “I understand your concern.”
lessons.quick: Gentleness isn’t weakness; it is having strength and choosing not to wound.
text: Remind them to be in subjection to rulers and to authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work,
to speak evil of no one, not to be contentious, to be gentle, showing all humility toward all men.
For we were also once foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.
But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared,
not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,
whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior;
that being justified by his grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

lessons.title: Abram Rebuked by Pharaoh
lessons.hear:
Abram is called the father of faith, yet he also had moments that make us cringe. During a famine he went down to Egypt and, afraid of being killed, told his wife Sarai to lie and say she was his sister. Sarai was taken into Pharaoh’s palace, and Pharaoh’s household was struck with plagues. Then came the most ironic scene of all: a pagan king summoned God’s servant and demanded, “What is this that you have done to me?” (Genesis 12:18).

A man who didn’t know God was giving a moral lecture to the one God had called. This is what a damaged witness looks like. Paul later quoted Scripture: “the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Romans 2:24). Our failures don’t only hurt us; they lead people to misunderstand God.

Today, review yourself honestly. Have coworkers heard me lie about why I need a day off? Have neighbors seen me be aggressive at an association meeting? Do friends find that I borrow things and don’t return them, or promise things and don’t follow through? Have people online seen me make snide remarks in the name of faith? Perhaps one day a friend who doesn’t believe will say to me, “How can you Christians be like this too?” That moment would be humiliating—but it might also be God’s gracious reminder.

Abram’s story didn’t end in Egypt. After he left, he went back “to the place of the altar, which he had made there at the first. There Abram called on the LORD’s name” (Genesis 13:4). The way to adjust is to return to the altar: confess before God, then make repairs before people. If your actions have hurt or disappointed a friend who doesn’t believe, the best witness is not to pretend nothing happened but to say plainly, “I was wrong about that. I’m sorry.” A Christian willing to admit wrong actually lets people see the reality of the gospel: we are not perfect people but people being changed by grace.
lessons.light: Abram lied out of fear—the self-protection of the self-centered life: save myself first and think about others later. Returning to the altar is returning to our proper place and letting God be God. Among the eight steps of changing a mindset, “review” and “adjustment” are part of our witness: those who admit their wrongs are the best witnesses to grace.
think: In Genesis 12:10-20, how did Abram’s fear affect his witness?
Is there a friend who doesn’t believe who has been disappointed in Christians because of my words or actions?
How will I “return to the altar” and make things right with that person?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that out of fear, convenience, or pride, I too have done things that brought dishonor to your name. Thank you that you didn’t give up on Abram, and you haven’t given up on me. Today I return to your altar and confess. Give me courage to say “I’m sorry” plainly to those who were affected. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of something that disappointed a friend who doesn’t believe. Today, confess it to God first; then, if it’s appropriate, apologize to that friend simply and tell them what you are willing to change.
lessons.quick: A Christian willing to admit wrong is the best witness to the reality of grace.
text: There was a famine in the land. Abram went down into Egypt to live as a foreigner there, for the famine was severe in the land.
When he had come near to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, “See now, I know that you are a beautiful woman to look at.
It will happen that when the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘This is his wife.’ They will kill me, but they will save you alive.
Please say that you are my sister, that it may be well with me for your sake, and that my soul may live because of you.”
When Abram had come into Egypt, some Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful.
The princes of Pharaoh saw her, and praised her to Pharaoh; and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house.
He dealt well with Abram for her sake. He had sheep, cattle, male donkeys, male servants, female servants, female donkeys, and camels.
The LORD afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife.
Pharaoh called Abram and said, “What is this that you have done to me? Why didn’t you tell me that she was your wife?
Why did you say, ‘She is my sister,’ so that I took her to be my wife? Now therefore, see your wife, take her, and go your way.”
Pharaoh commanded men concerning him, and they escorted him away with his wife and all that he had.

lessons.title: When Even the King Glorifies God
lessons.hear:
Daniel’s story ends with an unexpected royal decree. King Darius—who had been manipulated by scheming officials into throwing Daniel into the lions’ den—issued a decree to his whole kingdom: “men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel. For he is the living God, and steadfast forever. His kingdom is that which will not be destroyed” (Daniel 6:26).

Think about how that journey unfolded. Daniel didn’t hold an evangelistic rally or write articles criticizing the king. He simply served faithfully and honestly, day in and day out, for decades. When the ban came down, “he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before” (Daniel 6:10). It was precisely this “as he did before” kind of life that let a pagan king see the living God. This is what Peter meant: “they may see your good works and glorify God in the day of visitation” (1 Peter 2:12).

This week we have seen that we are pilgrims who must keep good behavior among the nations; that faithfulness in small things leaves no fault to be found; that we are to be gentle toward all in public; and that when we fail, we return to the altar and admit our wrong plainly. Now repeat it: each day as you leave work or school, take one minute to ask yourself, “Did anything I did today let people see Christ? Did anything bring dishonor to God’s name?”

Then multiply it. Character is mostly caught, not taught. You can take a younger coworker, a younger student, or your own child alongside you, and let them see how you report expenses honestly, respond gently, and apologize when you make a mistake. You can also share a real story of “choosing honesty” in your small group to encourage one another. When a whole community lives out good works, then just as with Daniel, even kings will give glory to God.
lessons.light: What Daniel lived out was ministry flowing from a changed way of living: not ministry first, but life first. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. In the 235, the most powerful inheritance spiritual parents pass on to spiritual children isn’t a lecture; it is letting the next generation see our faithfulness, “as he did before.”
think: In Daniel 6:25-28, why did King Darius give glory to God?
What habit in my life can I keep faithfully like Daniel, “as he did before”?
To which young person can I concretely pass on the witness of character?
lessons.speak: Father, Daniel made no loud proclamations, yet his lifetime of faithfulness let a king see you. Help me, in ordinary days, to pray, be honest, and be gentle just as I have done before, so that my coworkers, neighbors, and friends see my good works and give glory to you. Make me an example the next generation can follow. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite a young person (a coworker, younger student, or your child) to share a meal. Tell them about a time you chose honesty at work or in life, and pray for their workplace or campus.
lessons.quick: Faithfulness “as he did before” can let even a king see the living God.
text: Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages who dwell in all the earth: “Peace be multiplied to you.

“I make a decree that in all the dominion of my kingdom men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel. “For he is the living God, and steadfast forever. His kingdom is that which will not be destroyed. His dominion will be even to the end.
He delivers and rescues. He works signs and wonders in heaven and in earth, who has delivered Daniel from the power of the lions.”
So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

weeks.title: Ambassadors of Reconciliation
weeks.theme: Those whom God has reconciled are those whom God sends: a bridge between people and God, and between people and people, for Christ to walk across.
group: Read 2 Corinthians 5:17-21. Who does reconciliation come “of,” and what ministry have we been given in it?
Is there a broken relationship near you where you have been “waiting for the other person to speak first”?
Which two people (or which person and God) are you willing to build a bridge between this week, and what is your first step?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, invite a friend you haven’t been in touch with for a while—or someone you’ve had friction with—out for tea. Before you go, pray for three minutes, asking the Lord for a gentle heart and fitting words. When you meet, listen more and argue less; don’t rush to settle who was right, just let them know you value the relationship. Afterward, whatever the outcome, thank God that you were able to take this step.

lessons.title: All Things Are of God
lessons.hear:
We have walked through a whole year together, from “the Triune God is the source of all relationships” to today. If one word could gather up the whole year of social life, Paul gives it to us: reconciliation. He writes, “But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18).

Notice the order. Reconciliation did not begin with us. While we were still hiding, shifting blame, and each crowning ourselves king, God had already come toward us. He did not wait for our apology: “For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). The vertical beam of the cross joins heaven and earth; the horizontal beam joins person to person. Every reconciliation flows from the price God paid first.

Then Paul says something astonishing: “We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us” (2 Corinthians 5:20). An ambassador does not represent himself or promote himself; he carries the King’s word into hostile territory. Every sentence and every glance we offer at the office, in a group chat, or at a family gathering can become a channel through which God pleads with people to be reconciled.

This is an immense honor and a deep comfort. An ambassador’s authority does not rest on his own eloquence but on the One who sent him. You don’t have to become a perfect person before you can be an ambassador of reconciliation; you only have to be someone God has reconciled. A person who has been forgiven and welcomed home knows the way home better than anyone.
lessons.light: An ambassador’s proper place is to represent the King, not himself. The self-centered person in a conflict wants to win and be affirmed; the selfless ambassador has only one thing in mind: let Jesus reign, and bring both sides back before him. Change begins with me—first be reconciled, then urge others to be reconciled. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: the ambassador’s words come from a life that has been loved.
think: In 2 Corinthians 5:18-21, which actions of reconciliation does God himself perform?
Am I more like an ambassador, or like someone who only wants to defend himself?
Where today could I speak one word of reconciliation on Christ’s behalf?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you that while I was still your enemy, you reconciled me to yourself through Christ. You have entrusted me with the message of reconciliation, and I am truly unworthy. Take away my argumentative, score-keeping heart, and make me an ambassador who carries your heart among my family, co-workers, and friends. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Before bed tonight, write down three names: a friend who needs to be reconciled to God, someone you have friction with, and two relatives or friends who are estranged from each other. Pray for each name for one minute.
lessons.quick: Only those reconciled to God can urge others to be reconciled; an ambassador represents the King, not himself.
text: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.
But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation;
namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning to them their trespasses, and having committed to us the word of reconciliation.
We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us: we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

lessons.title: Once Useless, Now Useful
lessons.hear:
A brother who runs a small company in Taipei once had a young employee walk off with a large payment from a client and then disappear. Years later, that employee came to faith at a church retreat and sent word through a friend that he wanted to apologize in person. The brother’s first reaction was, “What good is an apology? That’s just the kind of person he’s always been.”

Our old mindset often says: a person is what he has done. Labeling people is the easiest and safest thing to do. But Philemon shows us God’s point of view. Onesimus was a runaway slave who very likely owed his master something, yet Paul writes that he “once was useless to you, but now is useful to you and to me” (Philemon 1:11). The name Onesimus means “useful”—God took a man who did not live up to his name and remade him into someone who did.

Paul does not lean on his apostolic authority to pressure Philemon. He says, “for love’s sake I rather appeal to you” (Philemon 1:9). This is the posture of an ambassador of reconciliation: not a judge, not a mere messenger, but someone standing between two people and loving them both. Paul even sees a bigger picture: “For perhaps he was therefore separated from you for a while that you would have him forever, no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:15-16).

The brother eventually agreed to meet, and he was wise about it: he accepted the apology but did not immediately hand the company’s finances back to the young man. Reconciliation takes time, and trust has to be rebuilt step by step. Yet that day, watching the man’s trembling hands, he suddenly understood: the work God was doing in this person was bigger than the money. He stopped looking only at “once” and began to see “now.”
lessons.light: Moving from a human point of view to God’s point of view means shifting from “who he used to be” to “what Christ is doing in him now.” The self-centered person condemns others by their past; the selfless person sees others through the cross. Forgiveness does not deny the harm, nor does it mean trust is instantly restored—but it opens a door so God’s new creation has room to happen.
think: In Philemon 1:8-16, how does Paul care for both Philemon and Onesimus at the same time?
Is there someone I keep seeing only through his “once”?
What one sentence could I say to affirm the change “now” at work in that person?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you did not condemn me by my past; you made me a new creation. Forgive me for so often labeling people and locking them in their past. Give me eyes that see your new creation, and give me wisdom to keep fitting boundaries even as I forgive. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of someone you have always written off as “just that kind of person.” Today, place his name before the Lord in prayer, and look for a chance to specifically affirm one small thing he has recently done right.
lessons.quick: God does not define people by their “once”; he remakes them by what Christ is doing “now.”
text: Therefore though I have all boldness in Christ to command you that which is appropriate,
yet for love’s sake I rather appeal to you, being such a one as Paul, the aged, but also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.
I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whom I have become the father of in my chains,
who once was useless to you, but now is useful to you and to me.
I am sending him back. Therefore receive him, that is, my own heart,
whom I desired to keep with me, that on your behalf he might serve me in my chains for the Good News.
But I was willing to do nothing without your consent, that your goodness would not be as of necessity, but of free will.
For perhaps he was therefore separated from you for a while that you would have him forever,
no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much rather to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

lessons.title: Put That to My Account
lessons.hear:
Paul’s letter to Philemon reaches its most moving point here: “If then you count me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. But if he has wronged you at all or owes you anything, put that to my account” (Philemon 1:17-18). This is what a real bridge looks like—a bridge has to bear the weight of both banks.

These two sentences are the gospel in miniature. Christ says the same thing before the Father: receive him as you would receive me; whatever he owes, charge it to me. We are accepted by God only because Someone paid our bill. So being an ambassador of reconciliation is not just saying a few nice words to make peace. It means being willing to pay a price for reconciliation: some time, some face, some risk of being misunderstood.

In a Chinese culture built on relationships and favors, this can be very concrete. When two elders in the family group chat fall out, you can visit each of them separately and listen to the hurt in their hearts, rather than taking sides in the chat. When two colleagues stop speaking to each other, you can invite them both to a meal—and pick up the bill yourself. When a friend has deep misunderstandings about the faith, you can start by apologizing for the ways the church has hurt him.

But be wise: building a bridge does not mean carrying everything for everyone. If money lending, violence, or any safety issue is involved, bring in a trusted elder, a pastor, or a professional, and don’t take the risk alone. An ambassador goes in the King’s authority, not in his own bravado. Paul closes by saying, “knowing that you will do even beyond what I say” (Philemon 1:21). When we take the first step, we often discover that God has already prepared far more in the other person’s heart.
lessons.light: Denying ourselves means living for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. “Put that to my account” is the signature of selfless love: not “I must win,” but “I am willing to take a loss so that both of them can come back before God.” People matter more than things; relationships matter more than possessions. Sometimes the price of one meal is the toll for crossing the bridge to reconciliation.
think: In Philemon 1:17-18, what is Paul willing to take on for Onesimus?
Where does my willingness to pay for reconciliation usually stop—at my pride, my time, or my money?
For which relationship could I pay a small “bridge toll” today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you said, “Put that to my account.” You paid every debt I owed. Make me willing to pay a price for the reconciliation of others, without keeping score and without showing off. Give me wisdom to discern when to draw near and when to ask others to come alongside. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Choose one strained relationship today (family, co-worker, or friend) and do one costly thing: invite them to a meal and pay, visit them in person, or be the first to say, “I’m sorry—I was wrong too.”
lessons.quick: A bridge bears the weight of both banks; an ambassador is willing to say, “Put that to my account.”
text: If then you count me a partner, receive him as you would receive me.
But if he has wronged you at all or owes you anything, put that to my account.
I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it (not to mention to you that you owe to me even your own self besides).
Yes, brother, let me have joy from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in the Lord.
Having confidence in your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even beyond what I say.

lessons.title: Sheathe Abishai’s Sword
lessons.hear:
On the day David fled in disgrace from his son Absalom, a man named Shimei followed along, cursing him and throwing stones at him (see 2 Samuel 16:5-7). Now the rebellion was over and David was returning to the capital, and Shimei rushed to be first in line to meet him. He fell before the king and said, “For your servant knows that I have sinned. Therefore behold, I have come today as the first of all the house of Joseph to go down to meet my lord the king” (2 Samuel 19:20).

Then Abishai, standing beside David, spoke up: “Shouldn’t Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD’s anointed?” (2 Samuel 19:21). It sounded reasonable—even “spiritual.” Beside almost every conflict stands an Abishai: “You can’t let someone like that off the hook,” “I’ve got your back—block him,” “You’re just too nice, that’s why people walk all over you.” Sometimes we are the Abishai beside someone else, using the language of justice to throw fuel on their anger.

But David said, “Shall any man be put to death today in Israel?” (2 Samuel 19:22). Then he swore to Shimei, “You will not die” (2 Samuel 19:23). An ambassador of reconciliation knows how to discern the times: today is a day of grace, not a day for settling scores.

Yet the story has a sequel. Years later, on his deathbed, David instructed Solomon about Shimei: “Now therefore don’t hold him guiltless” (1 Kings 2:9). Interpreters understand this differently; some read it in terms of national security and justice. But at the very least it reminds us: our lips can say “It’s fine,” while the ledger in our hearts never closes.

So today, sheathe Abishai’s sword in two places. First, in other people’s conflicts: when a friend pours out a grievance, don’t rush to sharpen his sword; walk with him in bringing the matter to God. Second, in your own heart: is there someone I say I have forgiven but am still quietly keeping accounts against? Forgiveness does not deny the harm, nor does it mean trust is instantly restored; but we can hand that ledger to the God who was “not reckoning to them their trespasses” (2 Corinthians 5:19).
lessons.light: Abishai’s sword is self-centered justice: making the other person pay so that I feel even. The ambassador of reconciliation returns to his proper place and leaves vengeance to God. Selflessness is not naivety; it is letting Jesus reign. On the cross he closed the ledger of my debts, so I can hand others’ accounts over to him as well.
think: In 2 Samuel 19:16-23, how do Abishai’s and David’s attitudes toward Shimei differ?
Have I ever played Abishai in someone else’s conflict, adding fuel to the fire?
Is there a ledger I claim to have closed but am still keeping, which I need to hand to God today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I am sometimes like Abishai, using righteous-sounding words to fuel other people’s anger; and sometimes I say I forgive while my heart is still keeping score. Thank you that on the cross you do not count my trespasses against me. Help me sheathe my sword and become a true ambassador of reconciliation. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If someone pours out a grievance to you today, don’t chime in with “You can’t let him get away with it.” Instead ask, “Could we pray about this together?” Before bed, write down one old account you are still keeping in your heart, and hand it to God in prayer.
lessons.quick: An ambassador doesn’t sharpen swords for others or secretly keep score.
text: Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjamite, who was of Bahurim, hurried and came down with the men of Judah to meet King David.

There were a thousand men of Benjamin with him, and Ziba the servant of Saul’s house, and his fifteen sons and his twenty servants with him; and they went through the Jordan in the presence of the king.
A ferry boat went to bring over the king’s household, and to do what he thought good. Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king when he had come over the Jordan.

He said to the king, “Don’t let my lord impute iniquity to me, or remember that which your servant did perversely the day that my lord the king went out of Jerusalem, that the king should take it to his heart.
For your servant knows that I have sinned. Therefore behold, I have come today as the first of all the house of Joseph to go down to meet my lord the king.”
But Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered, “Shouldn’t Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD’s anointed?”

David said, “What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should be adversaries to me today? Shall any man be put to death today in Israel? For don’t I know that I am king over Israel today?”
The king said to Shimei, “You will not die.” The king swore to him.

lessons.title: Barnabas: A Bridge Builder
lessons.hear:
After Saul came to faith and returned to Jerusalem, “he tried to join himself to the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple” (Acts 9:26). That made sense: not long before, this man had been arresting Christians. What a newly repentant person needs most is not more suspicion but someone willing to vouch for him.

“But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles” (Acts 9:27). The name Barnabas means “son of encouragement.” He did three things: he took Saul in, he brought him along, and he told his story. He first drew near to the one being shut out, then brought him into the community, and then spoke on his behalf about what God had done in him. This is what an ambassador of reconciliation looks like day to day—not necessarily standing at the pulpit, but often standing at the door, bringing people in.

And the result? Scripture says, “So the assemblies throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace and were built up” (Acts 9:31). One man built a bridge, and the Saul who was welcomed became the apostle Paul, who carried the gospel to the Gentiles. Reconciliation multiplies: those who have been welcomed go on to welcome the next person. When Paul later wrote asking Philemon to receive Onesimus, wasn’t he simply treating others the way Barnabas had once treated him?
