This week you have learned that all things are of God, to see people with new eyes, to pay a price for reconciliation, and to sheathe Abishai’s sword. Now pass on what you have received. Perhaps it is a newcomer at church who always sits in the back row; perhaps it is a colleague everyone at work ignores. You can be that person’s Barnabas. The experience of being welcomed is where a person is most likely to meet Christ.
lessons.light: The last step in changing a mindset is multiplication. Barnabas welcomed Saul, Saul welcomed Onesimus—one generation passing it to the next. This is also the seed of 235: one selfless companion can change the direction of someone’s whole life. When our focus is on Jesus, we are not afraid to vouch for others or to have our own reputation dragged down, because our guarantor is Christ himself.
think: What three things did Barnabas do for Saul in Acts 9:27?
On my own journey of faith, who has been a Barnabas to me?
Whom could I bring into a community this week who has been left out?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for sending people to be my Barnabas, welcoming me and leading me into your family. Make me a son of encouragement too—someone who notices those standing outside the door and is willing to vouch for them and bring them in. Let reconciliation keep flowing on through me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, send a message of thanks to someone who was a Barnabas to you. Then find a newcomer or someone who has been left out, invite them to a small group or a shared meal, and take the initiative to introduce them to everyone there.
lessons.quick: Barnabas took in, brought along, and spoke up; those who are welcomed go on to welcome the next person.
text: When Saul had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.

But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles, and declared to them how he had seen the Lord on the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
He was with them entering into Jerusalem,
preaching boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus. He spoke and disputed against the Hellenists, but they were seeking to kill him.
When the brothers knew it, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
So the assemblies throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace and were built up. They were multiplied, walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit.

weeks.keyText: We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us: we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.

weeks.title: 920: Fruit in Every Relationship
weeks.theme: Every person connected to me is a garden God has given me for bearing fruit; as I remain in the Lord, love grows naturally.
group: Read John 15:1-8. What is the branch’s secret to bearing fruit, and which word is repeated most?
Of the nine aspects of the fruit, which one is most lacking in which of your relationships, and why?
This week, in which of your “2s” do you want to bear which specific fruit?
weeks.sunday: Take a walk outdoors this weekend and notice a fruit-bearing tree or a potted plant. As you walk, pray one by one for the five “2s” in your life, asking the Holy Spirit to bring out one aspect of his fruit in each relationship. When you get home, choose one of them and drop off a small treat or write them a card. Finish by thanking God for all the relationships of this past week.

lessons.title: The Vine and the Branches
lessons.hear:
We have learned a lot this year: the life of love, the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit, our words, boundaries, friendship, neighbors, reconciliation. Now we want to tie it all together in one simple picture we can remember. On the night he was betrayed, as Jesus walked past the vineyards, he said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

The 321 Vision expresses this picture with three numbers: 920. The “2” is every person I am connected to—family, co-workers, neighbors, friends in my group chats, even the one who gives me headaches. The “0” is practicing selflessness: stepping back so that Christ can live in me. The “9” is the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit, which is the very life of Christ. In other words: in every “2,” through the “0,” the “9” grows.

Notice that a branch never has to grit its teeth and squeeze out grapes. It has only one job: stay on the vine. Sap flows from the root into the branch, and the fruit grows naturally. Our deepest exhaustion in relationships often comes from trying to squeeze out love and patience on our own. The secret Jesus gives is to “remain”—remain in prayer, remain in his word, remain in obedience.

The fruit is not for the branch itself. Grapes hang on the vine to be eaten, to benefit others. That is why Jesus says, “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit” (John 15:8). This is how our two core commitments come true: let Jesus reign, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Every one of your relationships can be a little vineyard where the Father’s glory is seen.
lessons.light: 920 is the whole year of social life distilled: the “2” is the garden, the “0” is the foundation, the “9” is the fruit. The self-centered person wants to produce fruit first in order to prove himself; the selfless person simply remains in the Lord and lets Christ’s life flow through. Life first, then relationships—fruit is the natural result of life, not a performance.
think: How many times does “remain” appear in John 15:1-8, and how is it related to bearing fruit?
How much of my exhaustion in relationships comes from trying to “squeeze out” love on my own?
How can I “remain” in the Lord for ten minutes today, even in the middle of a busy day?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the true vine and I am a branch. So often I try to hold up a good performance in my relationships by my own strength, and I end up tired and dry. Teach me to remain in you and let your life flow through me, bearing fruit in every person around me, so that the Father is glorified. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Over lunch or on your way home today, spend ten quiet minutes meditating on John 15:5. Then pray for one co-worker or family member you will see today, asking the Lord to let you bear one specific fruit toward them.
lessons.quick: A branch doesn’t squeeze out grapes; it remains on the vine, and the fruit grows naturally.
text: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer.
Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away. Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.
You are already pruned clean because of the word which I have spoken to you.
Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me.
I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
If a man doesn’t remain in me, he is thrown out as a branch and is withered; and they gather them, throw them into the fire, and they are burned.
If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you.
“In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples.

lessons.title: Fruit Is Not a Personality Trait
lessons.hear:
A brother working in Singapore is direct and efficiency-driven, and in his small group’s chat a single message from him often silences everyone. When someone gently pointed this out, he replied, “That’s just how I am. People need to get used to it.” A quiet, introverted sister was the opposite: she always felt she wasn’t “warm enough” and wasn’t fit to serve others. The two of them actually shared the same old mindset: my personality is my limit.

Paul sees it completely differently: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22-23). Notice that “fruit” is singular in the original. These are not nine gifts for different personalities to pick from; they are nine facets of one life. An extrovert doesn’t have to lose his enthusiasm, but gentleness will grow in him; an introvert doesn’t have to become a social butterfly, yet she can bear kindness and faithfulness.

How is that possible? Paul says, “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts” (Galatians 5:24). This is the “0” in 920: the old, self-centered self has been crucified with Christ, and the new life depends not on personality but on the Holy Spirit. Then he says, “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit” (Galatians 5:25). Since our life comes from the Spirit, our steps follow him too.

During a time of prayer, that brother was later nudged by the Holy Spirit: “Is your directness for the sake of truth, or for the sake of winning?” He began pausing for three seconds before sending a message, asking himself, “Which fruit will this sentence bear?” A few months later, his small group said he was “still very direct, but much warmer.” The Spirit didn’t erase his personality; he let the life of Christ shine through it.
lessons.light: “I was just born this way” sounds honest, but it is often the self-centered life’s protective charm. Selflessness doesn’t mean losing your personality; it means letting your personality be led by the Holy Spirit. From a human point of view to God’s: my limit is not my temperament but whether I am willing to let Jesus reign. When we rely on the Spirit with our hearts rather than on ourselves with our heads, fruit will grow right within the personality we already have.
think: In Galatians 5:24-26, how is bearing fruit related to being “crucified”?
Which “that’s just how I am” line do I most often use to refuse change?
Before I speak or send a message today, how can I pause three seconds to ask the Holy Spirit?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, I often use my personality as an excuse and refuse to let you change me. Please forgive me. Thank you that you don’t want to erase me but to bear the life of Christ within me. Today I want to walk by you, so that every word and every response carries the fragrance of your fruit. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in a group chat that often makes you impatient or makes you withdraw, pause three seconds before replying and ask, “Which fruit will this sentence bear?” Then revise one sentence before you send it.
lessons.quick: The nine-fold fruit is one life, not nine personalities; my limit is not my temperament but my surrender.
text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.
Let’s not become conceited, provoking one another, and envying one another.

lessons.title: Appointed to Bear Fruit
lessons.hear:
Jesus spoke words that are both warm and full of direction: “You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15:16). We didn’t sign ourselves up to be nice people; we were chosen and appointed by the Lord. Your office, your neighborhood, your extended family, your international student dorm—none of these are accidents. They are the vineyard the Lord has assigned to you.

Where does fruit grow? On real, specific people. Jesus goes on: “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you” (John 15:12). Love always has a name. Loving humanity in the abstract is easy. Loving the co-worker who is always late, the neighbor who always complains, the college roommate you haven’t contacted in six months—that is what bearing fruit really looks like.

That is why the “2” in 920 needs to be written down. For many people, a whole year goes by and their relationships are still stuck at “let’s catch up when we’re free.” Why not take a few minutes today for a simple review: 1. List the “2s” in your life—think of one or two people each from family, church, work, your neighborhood, and online. 2. Next to each name, write the one fruit they most need from you right now: patience? kindness? faithfulness? 3. Choose one person and act today.

You may worry, “I can’t do that much.” Remember, the Holy Spirit bears the fruit; you are only the branch. Jesus calls us friends, and he has made known to us everything he heard from the Father. We can likewise bring every name to him and ask, “Lord, how do you want me to love this person?” He delights to answer. One name, one fruit, one action—that is today’s vineyard.
lessons.light: The “2” in 920 is not a networking list but a trust assigned by God. Self-centered socializing asks, “Who is useful to me?” Selfless love asks, “Who needs the fruit of Christ?” People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Writing down names is handing those relationships over for Jesus to reign over, and it is the most concrete starting point for the daily See · Hear · Think · Speak · Do.
think: According to John 15:16, why did the Lord choose us, and what should our fruit do?
Which “2” in my life do I often overlook or merely put up with?
Toward which “2” will I bear which fruit today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for choosing me and appointing me to bear fruit. I bring every name in my life before you; please show me how to love each one. Give me strength to show concrete love to one of them today, so that your fruit may remain in their life. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in the app’s 920 Relationship Map, add a card for each of five “2s” and write a prayer for each. Then pick one of them and, before tonight, send a caring message or make a phone call.
lessons.quick: One name, one fruit, one action—that is today’s vineyard.
text: “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you.
Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.
You are my friends if you do whatever I command you.
No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.

You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain; that whatever you will ask of the Father in my name, he may give it to you.
“I command these things to you, that you may love one another.

lessons.title: Leave It One More Year
lessons.hear:
As the year draws to a close, looking back over our own vineyard can leave us uneasy: some relationships are colder than they were in January, some reconciliations haven’t even begun, and some promises never got past our lips. Jesus told a parable about a fig tree. For three years the owner came looking for fruit and found none, and he said, “Cut it down! Why does it waste the soil?” (Luke 13:7).

Those are heavy words, but the story doesn’t end there. The vine dresser answered, “Lord, leave it alone this year also, until I dig around it and fertilize it. If it bears fruit, fine” (Luke 13:8-9). This is the voice of grace. Our Lord is that vine dresser: he intercedes for us and grants us another year. He doesn’t simply leave us to ourselves; he personally loosens the soil, adds fertilizer, and deals with whatever is choking the roots.

Digging around the roots can hurt a little. In John’s Gospel, Jesus also says that the Father “prunes” every branch that bears fruit (John 15:2). As you take stock, honestly ask yourself three things: In which relationship is my self-centeredness most obvious—is it pride and saving face, keeping score, or needing to be needed? Whom have I kept avoiding instead of facing? Which fruit have I hardly borne at all this year?

Peter, too, denied the Lord three times, like a tree with no fruit at the critical moment. But the risen Lord prepared a charcoal fire for him by the sea and asked him three times, “Do you love me?” The Lord didn’t cut him down; he entrusted him with a new commission. Adjusting course does not mean blaming yourself until you are paralyzed; it means letting the Lord do the digging, and letting his grace become the fertilizer. “Leave it alone this year also”—that is what the Lord is saying to you today as well.
lessons.light: Reviewing is not condemnation; it is letting the Lord of the vineyard come in and loosen the soil. When the self-centered person fails, he makes excuses or pities himself; the selfless person says, “Lord, come and prune me.” Humility is the key to revival—admitting there is no fruit is exactly where fruit-bearing begins. God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.
think: In Luke 13:6-9, what does the vine dresser do for the fig tree?
Which relationship has been most lacking in fruit this year, and what role has my self-centeredness played in it?
Over the next month, where do I want to let the Lord “dig around” my roots?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that some of my relationships this year have not borne the fruit you desire. Thank you for not giving up on me, for still interceding for me and giving me another year. Dig up the hard soil in my heart; remove my pride, my score-keeping, and my avoidance, so that in the year ahead I may bear your fruit in the people around me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, spend fifteen minutes reflecting on the relationship you most regret this year. Write down one concrete step to make it right, and set a date to carry it out this week.
lessons.quick: The Lord doesn’t cut down the fruitless tree; he says, “Leave it one more year—I’ll loosen the soil.”
text: He spoke this parable. “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none.
He said to the vine dresser, ‘Behold, these three years I have come looking for fruit on this fig tree, and found none. Cut it down! Why does it waste the soil?’
He answered, ‘Lord, leave it alone this year also, until I dig around it and fertilize it.
If it bears fruit, fine; but if not, after that, you can cut it down.’”

lessons.title: Every Fruit Holds a Seed
lessons.hear:
Genesis 1 contains a beautiful detail. When God created the plants, he said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it” (Genesis 1:11). Inside the fruit is a seed. Real fruit is not only enjoyed—it multiplies.

That is exactly how the church in Colossae was born. Paul says the gospel had come to them, “even as it is in all the world and is bearing fruit and growing” (Colossians 1:6), and they had learned it from Epaphras. Epaphras was not famous, yet he carried the gospel he had received through Paul back to his own city. From prison, Paul prayed that they would be “bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God” (Colossians 1:10). One person received, and a whole city gained; one relationship bore fruit, and the next relationship received a seed.

This week we have learned to remain in the Lord, to let the Spirit work beyond our personality, to bear fruit in every “2,” and to let the Lord loosen our soil. Now pass 920 on. The most natural way is not to teach a lesson but to share a real story: “This week I learned patience with a co-worker, because…” When others hear your story, the seed falls into their hearts.

Perhaps you could invite a small group member or a family member to write down each other’s five “2s” and pray for one another for a month. That is multiplication: from one tree to a whole orchard. When the Lord comes, he will look for fruit in every one of our relationships. May he find not just a single piece of fruit, but an entire harvest.
lessons.light: The eight steps of changing a mindset end with multiplication. 920 is not one person’s private discipline but a seed that sprouts: my “2” may become the beginning of someone else’s “0” and “9.” Letting Jesus receive all the glory means letting the fruit keep growing, generation after generation.
think: In Colossians 1:5-10, how did the gospel travel through Epaphras to Colossae?
Which fruit that grew in me this week is worth sharing with others?
Whom could I invite to write down our five “2s” together and pray for each other for a month?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for putting seeds inside fruit so that life can go on. May what I have received this week not stop with me, but through my story and my companionship fall into someone else’s heart. Let 920 multiply in my home, my small group, and my workplace, so that your name is glorified. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, meet with a small group member or family member for twenty minutes and each share one fruit from your week. Then exchange the name of one of your “2s,” and agree to pray for each other’s friend for a month.
lessons.quick: Real fruit always holds a seed; plant the seed of 920 in the next person’s heart.
text: because of the hope which is laid up for you in the heavens, of which you heard before in the word of the truth of the Good News
which has come to you, even as it is in all the world and is bearing fruit and growing, as it does in you also, since the day you heard and knew the grace of God in truth,
even as you learned from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful servant of Christ on your behalf,
who also declared to us your love in the Spirit.
For this cause, we also, since the day we heard this, don’t cease praying and making requests for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,
that you may walk worthily of the Lord, to please him in all respects, bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God,

weeks.keyText: “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples.

weeks.title: 235: From Friends to Spiritual Companions
weeks.theme: The heavenly journey is not a solo marathon; find a selfless companion, support each other, and run toward the Lord together.
group: Read Ecclesiastes 4:9-12. What are the benefits of having a companion, and which one moves you most?
Have you had a spiritual companion in the past? What kept that journey together going—or brought it to an end?
Whom are you willing to invite to be your spiritual companion this week, and what will you do the first time you meet?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, meet for coffee with a brother or sister of the same sex whom you would like to invite to be your spiritual companion; choose a quiet but public place. Pray before you go. When you meet, each share the biggest change God has made in you this year, and then pray for each other. When you get home, write down three things you are thankful for, and set a time for your next meeting.

lessons.title: Two Are Better Than One
lessons.hear:
At the start of the year we read, “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18). When God made human beings, he placed them in relationships. Now that we have reached the ministry stage, we want to take this truth one step further: not merely to avoid being alone, but to have spiritual companions. Ecclesiastes says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor” (Ecclesiastes 4:9).

The Teacher lists three benefits of a companion. First, someone to help you up when you fall: “For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow” (Ecclesiastes 4:10). Second, warmth in the cold, like two people lying together at night and keeping warm. Third, help in battle: “If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him” (Ecclesiastes 4:12). Falling, cold, and attack—these are exactly what every Christian meets day after day at work, at home, and online.

The 321 Vision organizes godly relationships as “235”: the “2” is becoming spiritual companions with someone selfless; the “3” is building relationships of spiritual parents and children; the “5” is becoming comrades-in-arms on a five-fold ministry team. This week we focus on the “2.” A spiritual companion is not just a friend you get along with, but someone who keeps the focus on Jesus with you, who is honest with you, and who watches over you as you watch over them.

The last line of the passage is intriguing: “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclesiastes 4:12). Many preachers apply it to two people plus Christ. It is a beautiful application: true spiritual companions are not two people clinging tightly to each other, but two people clinging tightly to the Lord together. When Christ is in the middle, the cord can bear the heaviest strains of life.
lessons.light: The “2” in 235 is walking with someone selfless. Self-centered friendship slides into dependence or comparison, but a selfless companion brings the other person back to Jesus. The focus is on Jesus—not on ourselves, not on each other. He is the third strand of the cord, keeping our journey together from becoming mutual bondage and turning it instead into a strength that frees us and lets us overcome together.
think: What benefits of a companion are listed in Ecclesiastes 4:9-12?
The last time I “fell,” who was there to help me up?
Who in my life might become the companion who holds on to the Lord with me?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you that you don’t make me run the heavenly race alone. I confess that I am used to holding it all together by myself and not letting anyone see my weakness. Please provide a selfless spiritual companion for me, and make me a companion for others, with Christ as the third strand of the cord between us. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Take some quiet time today to write down the names of two or three brothers or sisters of the same sex whom you trust and who are spiritually mature. Pray for each of them for one minute, asking the Lord to show you whom to invite to walk with you.
lessons.quick: Two are better than one; in a threefold cord, the middle strand is Christ.
text: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone?
If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

lessons.title: Sent Out Two by Two
lessons.hear:
A sister who went to New Zealand for graduate school came to faith far from home and took it very seriously: she read the Bible every day and watched the livestreamed sermon online every Sunday. She often said, “My faith is between me and God. I don’t need to bother anyone.” Then one winter, hit by pressure in her studies and a painful breakup at the same time, she didn’t open her Bible for an entire month—and no one knew.

Our old mindset says: a mature Christian should be independent and not need anyone else. But look at what Jesus did: “the Lord also appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two ahead of him” (Luke 10:1). He could have scattered the seventy to seventy different places—far more efficient. Instead he chose to send them two by two. In God’s kingdom, walking together is itself part of the ministry.

Jesus also said, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Luke 10:2). Facing an enormous need, he didn’t tell his disciples to work overtime; he told them to pray first. Two people praying together, entering a home together, saying together, “Peace be to this house,” become each other’s witnesses and protectors. Jesus said plainly, “I send you out as lambs among wolves” (Luke 10:3)—which is all the more reason to have a companion.

Eventually another sister studying abroad noticed what was going on, and the two of them began meeting by video call for thirty minutes each week: reading a passage, sharing one struggle, and praying for each other. She said, “I used to think independence was maturity. Now I know that being willing to let others see my weakness is real humility.” If low moods persist, seeking counseling or medical help is also God’s grace—and a spiritual companion is often the first person to notice you need help.
lessons.light: “I can handle it myself” looks strong, but it is often self-centered pride: not wanting anyone to see our weakness, not wanting to owe anyone. Humility is returning to our proper place—I am a creature, made to walk with others. Letting people be people and God be God includes giving others the chance to love me; accepting help is also a practice of letting Jesus reign.
think: In Luke 10:1-3, why did Jesus send the disciples out two by two?
Do I often say, “I don’t want to bother anyone”? What is the real reason behind it?
Whom could I tell honestly about one of my recent struggles this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you sent your disciples out two by two, yet I so often try to carry everything alone. Forgive me for mistaking independence for maturity and not asking for help for spirituality. Give me a humble heart, willing to be seen and supported by others, and willing to support others too. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message to a brother or sister you trust. Honestly share one recent struggle and ask them to pray for you for a week; then ask them, “Is there anything I can pray for you about?”
lessons.quick: Jesus sent them out two by two; being willing to let others see our weakness is true humility.
text: Now after these things, the Lord also appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he was about to come.
Then he said to them, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest, that he may send out laborers into his harvest.
Go your ways. Behold, I send you out as lambs among wolves.
Carry no purse, nor wallet, nor sandals. Greet no one on the way.
Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house.’
If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; but if not, it will return to you.
Remain in that same house, eating and drinking the things they give, for the laborer is worthy of his wages. Don’t go from house to house.

lessons.title: Invite a Spiritual Companion
lessons.hear:
Sitting in prison, Paul wrote to the church in Philippi, and his very first words were, “I thank my God whenever I remember you” (Philippians 1:3). This is spiritual companionship at its warmest: whenever you think of the other person, your heart fills with thanks. They were so close because of their “partnership in furtherance of the Good News from the first day until now” (Philippians 1:5). The heart of companionship is not simply enjoying each other’s company but moving toward the gospel together.

Today we want to turn the “2” from a wish into an action: invite a spiritual companion. How do you choose? Look for three marks. 1. Selfless: in conversation, their focus is usually on Jesus and on others, not always on themselves. 2. Trustworthy: they can keep your confidences and won’t turn prayer requests into gossip. 3. Walking forward: they also long to grow and are willing to meet regularly. For purity and safety, a close companion should be of the same sex. A husband and wife are, of course, each other’s closest companions, but it is still worthwhile for each to have a spiritual friend of the same sex.

The invitation doesn’t have to be formal. You might simply say, “I want to take my faith more seriously. Would you be willing to meet with me for thirty minutes every week or every other week to read a passage and pray for each other? Let’s try it for three months.” That gives you both a beginning, and a point at which to review how it is going.

Paul also said, “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). This is the most important conviction between companions: I am not your savior or your supervisor; I am someone who believes with you that God will surely complete his work in us. You will fall together, get up together, and see God’s faithfulness together.
lessons.light: Inviting a companion is an act of humility, because you are admitting that you need others. A selfless companionship does not run on feelings but on a shared focus: let Jesus reign. Life first, then relationships, then ministry—only when two lives are being built up together does ministry have a foundation. A companion is the first brick of 235.
think: In Philippians 1:3-8, what was the relationship between Paul and the Philippians built on?
When I look for a companion, do I value easy conversation more, or the direction of their life?
Whom will I invite, and what words will I use to ask?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for the brothers and sisters you have placed around me. Guide me to a selfless spiritual companion, and give me the courage to ask. May our journey together be centered on you; may we watch over each other and pray for each other, confident that you will complete the good work you have begun in us. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, by message or in person, invite a brother or sister of the same sex to be your spiritual companion for three months, meeting for thirty minutes every week or every other week. Agree on the time and place of your first meeting.
lessons.quick: A spiritual companion is not just someone easy to talk to, but someone moving toward the gospel with you.
text: I thank my God whenever I remember you,
always in every request of mine on behalf of you all, making my requests with joy,
for your partnership in furtherance of the Good News from the first day until now;
being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.

It is even right for me to think this way on behalf of all of you, because I have you in my heart, because both in my bonds and in the defense and confirmation of the Good News, you all are partakers with me of grace.
For God is my witness, how I long after all of you in the tender mercies of Christ Jesus.

lessons.title: Couldn’t You Watch One Hour?
lessons.hear:
In the Garden of Gethsemane, Jesus took Peter, James, and John further in with him. He said to them, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch” (Mark 14:34). It is a stunning picture: the Son of God, in his hour of greatest anguish, longed for companions to stay with him.

But the disciples fell asleep—once, twice, three times. Jesus came back and said, “Simon, are you sleeping? Couldn’t you watch one hour?” And then, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mark 14:37-38). The Lord did not rebuke them for disloyalty; instead, he named their real condition: their hearts wanted to stay with him, but their bodies couldn’t hold out.

We are often like this as companions. A friend sends a message late at night; we see it and think, “I’ll reply tomorrow.” We promise to pray for someone and forget as soon as we get busy. Someone is suffering, and we rush to give advice just so we can stop feeling uncomfortable. The opposite failure also happens: treating our companion as our personal life preserver, expecting a response at any hour, and feeling hurt whenever comfort doesn’t come right away. The first is indifference, the second is dependence, but both are rooted in self-centeredness.

The way to adjust is found in Jesus’ last words in the scene: “Arise! Let’s get going” (Mark 14:42). The Lord did not cancel their journey together because the disciples failed; he took them with him and kept moving forward. Today, if you have fallen asleep when a companion needed you, go and say you’re sorry. If you have made a companion into your god, hand that weight back to the Lord. A good companion is not on call twenty-four hours a day, but upholds the other in prayer and entrusts them to the God who never slumbers.
lessons.light: Indifference and dependence are both self-centered: one cares only for its own convenience, the other only for its own needs. A selfless companion can stay close and also understands boundaries—entrusting the other person to God rather than becoming their god. This is returning to our proper place: let people be people, and let God be God. A companion can walk part of the road with you, but only the Lord can carry you the whole way.
think: In Mark 14:32-42, how does Jesus’ attitude toward the disciples change each of the three times he returns?
As a companion, do I tend more toward indifference or toward dependence?
To whom do I need to say I’m sorry, or what weight do I need to hand back to God?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, in Gethsemane you longed for someone to stay with you, and the disciples fell asleep; I am often the one who falls asleep too. Forgive my indifference, and forgive my weakness of leaning on people instead of you. Teach me to stay watchful in prayer, and to be a companion who is present and who also keeps healthy boundaries. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of a friend you “slept through” when they needed you. Send a message to apologize and ask how they are doing. Or write down one expectation you have been placing too heavily on someone, and hand it to the Lord in prayer.
lessons.quick: The Lord didn’t cancel the journey because his disciples slept; he said, “Arise! Let’s get going.”
text: They came to a place which was named Gethsemane. He said to his disciples, “Sit here while I pray.”
He took with him Peter, James, and John, and began to be greatly troubled and distressed.
He said to them, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch.”
He went forward a little, and fell on the ground, and prayed that if it were possible, the hour might pass away from him.
He said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible to you. Please remove this cup from me. However, not what I desire, but what you desire.”
He came and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, “Simon, are you sleeping? Couldn’t you watch one hour?
Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
Again he went away and prayed, saying the same words.
Again he returned and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy; and they didn’t know what to answer him.
He came the third time and said to them, “Sleep on now, and take your rest. It is enough. The hour has come. Behold, the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.
Arise! Let’s get going. Behold, he who betrays me is at hand.”

lessons.title: Strengthened in God
lessons.hear:
David was being hunted by Saul and was hiding in the woods of the wilderness of Ziph. It was the loneliest and most dangerous moment of his life. Just then, Jonathan got up and went to find him. Scripture describes that visit in a single sentence: “Jonathan, Saul’s son, arose and went to David into the woods, and strengthened his hand in God” (1 Samuel 23:16).

Look closely at that sentence. Jonathan didn’t bring David an army or solve his problems for him; he brought David’s heart back to God. He said, “Don’t be afraid,” and reminded David of God’s promise: “you will be king over Israel, and I will be next to you” (1 Samuel 23:17). The greatest gift a true spiritual companion gives is not getting you to lean on him, but helping you lean more on God. This was Jonathan’s selflessness: he could have been heir to the throne, yet he gladly chose to stand next to David instead.

This week we have seen that two are better than one, that the Lord sends his people out two by two, how to invite a companion, and how to start walking together again after failure. Now it is time to multiply. Once you have a companion, don’t let the blessing stop between the two of you. You could each invite one more person and form a group of three. Or go together to visit a friend who is out “in the woods”—someone who has lost a job, is newly divorced, or is lonely in a foreign land—and bring God’s word to strengthen them.

This is how the life of 235 flows: companionship (2) naturally grows into relationships of spiritual parents and children (3), and then into a team that serves together (5). You don’t need to wait until you are perfect to begin. Jonathan made just one trip into the woods, yet he left a permanent mark on David’s life. Today, who in the woods near you is waiting for a Jonathan?
lessons.light: Jonathan is a model of the selfless companion: not grasping for the throne, only helping his friend fulfill God’s call; not making people lean on him, but helping them lean on God. This is the “2” of 235: the destination of companionship is not each other but Christ. Changing a mindset ends in multiplication—those who have been strengthened go on to strengthen the next person.
think: In 1 Samuel 23:16-17, how did Jonathan “strengthen his hand in God”?
In my loneliest time, who came looking for me like Jonathan did?
Whom “in the woods” could my companion and I visit together this week?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for sending people like Jonathan into my woods. Make me that kind of companion too—not getting people to lean on me, but strengthening them to lean on you. Lead my companion and me to visit those in need together, so that the blessing of walking together keeps multiplying. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, together with your spiritual companion, visit or meet up with a friend who is going through a low season (during the day, in a public place). Bring a verse of promise, listen to them, and pray for them.
lessons.quick: A good companion doesn’t get people to lean on him, but strengthens them to lean on God.
text: David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life. David was in the wilderness of Ziph in the woods.
Jonathan, Saul’s son, arose and went to David into the woods, and strengthened his hand in God.
He said to him, “Don’t be afraid, for the hand of Saul my father won’t find you; and you will be king over Israel, and I will be next to you; and Saul my father knows that also.”
They both made a covenant before the LORD. Then David stayed in the woods and Jonathan went to his house.

weeks.keyText: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.

weeks.title: Spiritual Parents and Comrades-in-Arms
weeks.theme: Life is passed on by walking alongside, not by lecturing; those who have been supported must support the next generation, and together we become good soldiers of the Lord.
group: Read 2 Timothy 2:1-2. How many generations can you find in these two verses?
Who has been a spiritual parent to you, and what about them has influenced you most?
Which younger believer are you willing to take the initiative to walk alongside this week, and how do you plan to begin?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, invite a younger believer (or a young family) for a simple meal at your home or at a restaurant—ideally hosting together with your spouse or companion. Pray together before the meal, and during it share the story of how you came to faith and the times you have stumbled. As you part, bless them. When you get home, thank God for this time together and mark a date on your calendar to reach out again.

lessons.title: Entrust It to Faithful People
lessons.hear:
When Paul wrote 2 Timothy, he already knew his death was near. In a spiritual father’s last letter, what weighed most on his heart? He wrote, “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). This one short verse holds four generations: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, and others. The gospel is not a treasure to be stored away but a relay, passed from one runner to the next.

Last week we talked about the “2” in 235—spiritual companions. This week we move on to the “3” and the “5.” The “3” is the relationship of spiritual parents and children: someone further along the road walking alongside those coming behind. Paul called Timothy “my child”; this was not a job title but a bond of love and responsibility. Timothy’s faith had a history, too: it lived first in his grandmother and mother (see 2 Timothy 1:5), and then was nurtured by Paul.

The “5” is comrades-in-arms on a five-fold ministry team. Paul goes on with three images: the soldier, the athlete, and the hardworking farmer (see 2 Timothy 2:3-6). The soldier must endure hardship with others; the athlete must compete by the rules; the farmer must labor patiently. All three pictures show that ministry is not a solo performance by a hero, but faithful, long-term giving of ourselves within a team.

Where does the strength for all this come from? Paul says it in his very first line: “You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 2:1). Not strong in our own abilities, but strong in grace. You don’t have to become a perfect spiritual parent first; you only need to faithfully pass on to the next person what you have received from the Lord.
lessons.light: The “3” and “5” of 235 are the passing on of life and partnership in a team. Self-centered service wants to build its own reputation; selfless service only wants to pass on the life of Christ. The last step in changing a mindset is multiplication—passing it on is life’s greatest fruit, and it is the framework for building God’s system.
think: In 2 Timothy 2:1-7, what three images does Paul use to describe those who serve?
Do I tend to think that passing on the faith is the pastor’s job and has nothing to do with me?
What have I received from the Lord that I could entrust to a younger person?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for bringing the gospel to me through so many people. I don’t want the relay to stop in my hands. Strengthen me in the grace that is in Christ, help me find a faithful person, and let me entrust to him what I have received. And make me a faithful, good soldier on your team. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, sketch a simple “spiritual family tree”: who led you to faith, who discipled you, and whom you have walked alongside. Pray with thanks for each name, and in the next box write the name of someone you would like to walk alongside.
lessons.quick: The gospel is a relay; be strong in grace and pass what you have received to the next runner.
text: You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.
The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.
You therefore must endure hardship as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
No soldier on duty entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier.
Also, if anyone competes in athletics, he isn’t crowned unless he has competed by the rules.
The farmer who labors must be the first to get a share of the crops.
Consider what I say, and may the Lord give you understanding in all things.

lessons.title: Not Many Fathers
lessons.hear:
A retired sister in Kuala Lumpur has been a believer for over thirty years; she has taught Sunday school and sung in the choir. When her small group leader asked her to walk alongside a young mother who had just come to faith, she quickly waved it off: “I didn’t go to seminary, and I can’t explain the Bible well. You should ask the pastor.”

Our old mindset says spiritual parents must be very knowledgeable and gifted teachers. But Paul says something striking: “For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers” (1 Corinthians 4:15). Tutors pass on knowledge; parents pass on life. Today we are flooded with information—sermons, courses, and videos without end. What is truly lacking is not tutors, but parents willing to walk alongside over the long haul and let others see their lives up close.

Paul goes on, “I beg you therefore, be imitators of me” (1 Corinthians 4:16). It sounds bold, but it is actually humble and down-to-earth: so much of spiritual growth is caught by watching and learning. A young mother may not need a complete sermon. She needs to see how a sister stays thankful when her husband loses his job, and keeps praying when her child rebels. Paul also sent Timothy, “who will remind you of my ways which are in Christ” (1 Corinthians 4:17).

In the end, the retired sister agreed. Every other week she simply met the young mother at a park near her home, playing with the kids while they talked and prayed. A year later, the young mother shared in small group, “She never gave me a lesson, but from her I learned how to be a Christian mom.” It turns out that the qualification for a spiritual parent is not perfection, but being real and being willing.
lessons.light: “I’m not good enough” sounds humble, but sometimes it is another form of self-centeredness—the fear of exposing our imperfections. Humility is returning to our proper place: I am not the Savior, just someone changed by grace, willing to let others see up close what Christ has done in me. Life shapes life; this is what the 321 Vision means by “life first.”
think: In 1 Corinthians 4:15, what is the difference between “tutors” and “fathers”?
Have I used “I’m not good enough” as an excuse not to walk alongside others?
Which real experience in my life could be a help to someone else?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I often feel I am not good enough and not worthy to walk alongside others. Thank you for reminding me that the qualification for a spiritual parent is not perfection, but being real and willing. Use my ordinary life so that a young believer can see your grace and faithfulness in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, ask your small group leader or pastor, “Is there someone who just came to faith or just arrived who needs someone to walk alongside them?” If so, ask them to introduce you, and arrange a first conversation with someone of the same sex in a public place.
lessons.quick: There are ten thousand tutors but not many fathers; a spiritual parent’s qualification is being real and willing.
text: I don’t write these things to shame you, but to admonish you as my beloved children.
For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News.
I beg you therefore, be imitators of me.
Because of this I have sent Timothy to you, who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, who will remind you of my ways which are in Christ, even as I teach everywhere in every assembly.

lessons.title: Like a Mother, Like a Father
lessons.hear:
When Paul describes how he shepherded the Thessalonians, he uses two homely pictures. One is a mother: “But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children” (1 Thessalonians 2:7). The other is a father: “we exhorted, comforted, and implored every one of you, as a father does his own children” (1 Thessalonians 2:11). Spiritual parents need both: a mother’s gentle nurture and a father’s encouragement and direction.

Even more important is verse 8: “we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls” (1 Thessalonians 2:8). Spiritual companionship is not just passing on knowledge; it is sharing life—your time, your home, your dinner table, even your failures. Children don’t learn to talk in a classroom; they learn around the family table.

How can you start today? Here are three simple steps. 1. Find someone: a believer of the same sex who is younger than you or newer to the faith. 2. Meet once: share a meal, take a walk, or do chores together. You don’t need an agenda; just let them feel cared for. 3. Ask a question: “Is there anything about your faith lately that confuses you, or where you’d like to go deeper?” Then listen quietly, and close by praying for them.

At the same time, don’t forget the other side: you need spiritual parents too. If there is an older believer you respect, go and seek their counsel today as well. For wisdom and protection, close mentoring is best done with someone of the same sex, in a public setting or with others around. Don’t take on counseling beyond your ability; when serious emotional or family problems come up, invite a pastor or a professional to help. Spiritual parents walk alongside; they are not all-powerful rescuers.
lessons.light: “Not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls”—this is self-denial: living for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. Rely on the Spirit with your heart rather than on yourself with your head. Spiritual parenting doesn’t depend on technique but on a heart compelled by Christ’s love, bringing people to Jesus so that he reigns—rather than getting people to follow us.
think: In 1 Thessalonians 2:7-12, what did Paul do like a mother, and what did he do like a father?
Am I better at gentle nurture or at encouragement and direction, and which one am I lacking?
Which younger believer will I reach out to today, and how?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, you love me with a father’s heart and uphold me with a mother’s gentleness. Make me willing to share my life with others—not only teaching, but also my time and my heart. Give me wisdom and a sense of proportion, so that I know how to walk alongside people and when I need to ask others to help. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, contact a believer of the same sex who is younger than you, and arrange to share a meal or take a thirty-minute walk this week. Ask them, “Is there anywhere in your faith you’d like to go deeper lately?” When they finish, pray for them.
lessons.quick: Spiritual parents give not only the gospel but their own lives.
text: But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.
Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.
For you remember, brothers, our labor and travail; for working night and day, that we might not burden any of you, we preached to you the Good News of God.
You are witnesses with God how holy, righteously, and blamelessly we behaved ourselves toward you who believe.
As you know, we exhorted, comforted, and implored every one of you, as a father does his own children,
to the end that you should walk worthily of God, who calls you into his own Kingdom and glory.

lessons.title: Too Heavy to Carry Alone
lessons.hear:
Moses was a great leader, yet he was nearly crushed by his ministry. “The people stood around Moses from the morning to the evening,” waiting for him alone to judge their cases. His father-in-law Jethro saw it and asked a pointed question: “Why do you sit alone?” Then he said, “The thing that you do is not good. You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone” (Exodus 18:17-18).

Many zealous Christians are modern-day versions of Moses. They handle every detail of the small group themselves, personally reply to every message in the group chat, and the newcomers only know them. On the surface it looks like responsibility, but underneath there may be self-centeredness: “It has to be me,” “Others won’t do it right,” “I am needed, so I matter.” The result is not only that they burn out, but that those they are mentoring never grow up, because no one gives them a chance.

The other failure is control. Some spiritual parents keep their spiritual children tied to their side, need to weigh in on everything, and can’t stand it when the children learn from others. That is really putting ourselves in God’s place. Paul puts it well: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Spiritual parents are only gardeners, not the masters of anyone’s life.

Moses’ adjustment is beautiful: he was willing to listen to his father-in-law. Jethro taught him to choose “able men which fear God: men of truth” (Exodus 18:21) to share the responsibility, so that “they shall share the load with you” (Exodus 18:22). This is the move from parents to comrades-in-arms: raising people up to stand shoulder to shoulder with you. A humble leader is not the one who does the most, but the one who lets the most people serve together.
lessons.light: “It has to be me” is leaving our proper place and grasping power; sharing the load and letting go is laying power down and returning to our proper place. Humility breeds humility—when I let others serve alongside me, they grow up through serving. Letting Jesus reign means admitting that I am only one member of his team; the glory goes to God, not to me.
think: In Exodus 18:13-23, what problems did Jethro see in Moses, and what solution did he propose?
In serving or walking alongside others, do I have an “it has to be me” or controlling attitude?
What task could I hand to someone else, or for which young person could I open a door?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that sometimes I want to do everything myself, as if it all depends on me; and sometimes I want to control other people’s growth. Forgive my pride. Thank you for reminding me through Jethro that the work is too heavy for me to carry alone. Make me humble enough to take advice, to share the load, and to let go. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, look over one area of ministry or household responsibility you are carrying. Choose one task to hand over to a younger person, and stay beside them the first time they do it; afterward, specifically affirm what they did well.
lessons.quick: A humble leader is not the one who does the most, but the one who lets the most people serve together.
text: On the next day, Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from the morning to the evening.

When Moses’ father-in-law saw all that he did to the people, he said, “What is this thing that you do for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people stand around you from morning to evening?”
Moses said to his father-in-law, “Because the people come to me to inquire of God.
When they have a matter, they come to me, and I judge between a man and his neighbor, and I make them know the statutes of God, and his laws.”
Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “The thing that you do is not good.
You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone.
Listen now to my voice. I will give you counsel, and God be with you. You represent the people before God, and bring the causes to God.
You shall teach them the statutes and the laws, and shall show them the way in which they must walk, and the work that they must do.

Moreover you shall provide out of all the people able men which fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.

Let them judge the people at all times. It shall be that every great matter they shall bring to you, but every small matter they shall judge themselves. So shall it be easier for you, and they shall share the load with you.
If you will do this thing, and God commands you so, then you will be able to endure, and all these people also will go to their place in peace.”

lessons.title: Every Joint Supplies
lessons.hear:
Paul says that the ascended Christ gave all kinds of gifts: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers” (Ephesians 4:11). The 321 Vision calls this the five-fold ministry team. Different traditions understand the present-day form of these roles differently, but all agree on their purpose: “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12). These ministries are not for a few people to perform, but to equip everyone to take the field.

This is exactly the “5” in 235: comrades-in-arms. Picture an orchestra: someone pioneers new music (apostle), someone keeps the direction clear (prophet), someone brings newcomers in (evangelist), someone cares for everyone (shepherd), and someone explains the score clearly (teacher). Each one is different, yet they all play the same piece. Spiritual comrades-in-arms don’t compete over whose position matters most; instead, “speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ” (Ephesians 4:15).

This week we have walked a path: entrusting the faith to faithful people, being real spiritual parents, walking alongside others like a mother and a father, and learning to share the load and let go. Now we weave it all into one fabric: “from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love” (Ephesians 4:16). Every joint matters, and you are one of them.

Pass on what you have received this week. Tell your companion or small group, “I think my gifting might be in this area—would you help me see if that’s true?” And help others discover their gifts. When everyone finds their place, the church is no longer a crowd of spectators but a team fighting side by side, building God’s system together with one heart.
lessons.light: Building God’s system doesn’t depend on one super-leader but on what every joint supplies. Selfless people don’t fight for position; they simply ask, “Lord, where can I best build others up?” From companions (2) to spiritual parents and children (3) to comrades-in-arms (5), the body of Christ grows up in love, and the Lord’s Prayer is gradually fulfilled among us.
think: In Ephesians 4:11-16, what is the purpose of the various ministries?
Which gifting do I lean toward, and have I ever looked down on myself or others because of comparison?
How can I help a fellow member of the body discover and use their gift?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the head, and we are all members of your body. Thank you for giving all kinds of gifts to equip the saints. Help me find my place, and gladly help others find theirs, so that we support one another in love and build up your body together as comrades-in-arms fighting side by side. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, at small group or when you meet your companion, name a specific gift you see in another believer—for example, “I see how well you care for newcomers.” Encourage them to try using it next month.
lessons.quick: The church is not a crowd of spectators but comrades-in-arms, with every joint doing its part.
text: He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers;
for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ,
until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,
that we may no longer be children, tossed back and forth and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the trickery of men, in craftiness, after the wiles of error;
but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,

from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love.

weeks.keyText: The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.

weeks.title: Let Jesus Reign in Our Relationships
weeks.theme: When Jesus reigns in every one of my relationships, the kingdom of heaven comes down to our dinner tables, group chats, and neighborhoods.
group: Read Matthew 6:9-13. How many times does “us” or “our” appear in the Lord’s Prayer, and what does that remind us about social life?
Looking back over this year, which part of the five-fold change—mindset, life, living, relationships, ministry—has been most visible? Tell a story.
Which two or three people are you willing to form a 235 spiritual companions group with, and toward which neighbor will you take your first step of love this week?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, hold a simple “sending meal” with your spiritual companions or small group. Everyone brings a dish; take turns sharing one way God showed you grace in your relationships this year, and then write down five names you will walk alongside next year. Finish by laying hands on one another or praying in a circle, sending each person back into their family, workplace, and community as ambassadors of reconciliation. Close by singing a song of thanksgiving together.

lessons.title: Let Your Kingdom Come
lessons.hear:
A year-long journey comes to its close in the Lord’s Prayer. Jesus taught us to pray, “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10). We have said these words countless times, but have you ever asked: where is God’s kingdom supposed to come? Not only in the distant future, but today—in your home, your office, your messaging groups, your neighborhood association.

Notice the pronouns in the Lord’s Prayer. Jesus didn’t teach us to say “my Father” but “Our Father in heaven”; not “give me” but “give us.” From beginning to end, the Lord’s Prayer is a prayer of relationships. The most concrete line is this one: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12). The coming of the kingdom often begins with a single act of forgiveness, a single reconciliation.

The 321 Vision says that the purpose of our whole life is to build God’s system: to establish God’s domain on earth so that the Lord’s Prayer is fulfilled—God’s name kept holy, God’s kingdom come, God’s will done on earth as it is in heaven. It sounds grand, but it is actually very everyday. When you stop judging at a family gathering, God’s name is kept holy. When you speak up for an overlooked colleague at work, God’s kingdom comes. When you choose forgiveness over revenge, God’s will is done on earth.

The ending of the Lord’s Prayer brings everything back to the throne: “For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever” (Matthew 6:13). These are our two core commitments: let Jesus reign, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The deepest healing in our relationships doesn’t come from learning more techniques, but from stepping off the throne and letting the true King sit at the center of every relationship.
lessons.light: Building God’s system begins with our relationships: letting Jesus reign in each one. The self-centered person wants to be king in his relationships, expecting others to listen and comply; the selfless person gives up the throne and lets the order of heaven—love, forgiveness, humility—rule between people. This is how the Lord’s Prayer is fulfilled on earth.
think: Which lines in Matthew 6:9-13 bear directly on how I get along with others?
In which relationship do I still want to sit on the throne?
Where today could I let God’s kingdom come, even a little?
lessons.speak: Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy; may your kingdom come in my home, my work, and every relationship around me. I choose to step off the throne and let the Lord Jesus reign. Forgive my debts, and make me glad to forgive those who are in debt to me. Yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This morning, pray through the Lord’s Prayer line by line for three people: a family member, a co-worker, and a neighbor. For each, pray, “Let your kingdom come in his (or her) life,” and speak a word of blessing to one of them during the day.
lessons.quick: The Lord’s Prayer is an “us” prayer; when Jesus reigns in each relationship, the kingdom comes.
text: Pray like this: “‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’

lessons.title: That the World May Believe
lessons.hear:
At the start of this journey we read Jesus’ high priestly prayer and saw that the Triune God is the source of all relationships. Coming back to it a year later, you will notice something new. Jesus said, “Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one” (John 17:20-21). You and I are those “who will believe in me through their word.” Two thousand years ago, the Lord was already praying for our relationships today.

Our old mindset often says: faith is between me and God, and unity is the church leaders’ business. A brother working in Shanghai thought exactly that. His fellowship had split into two camps over how serving roles were assigned, and the group chat was full of cold, cutting remarks. He chose to stay silent, thinking, “I’ll just take care of myself.” Then one day a co-worker who was exploring the faith said to him, “You Christians talk about love, but you can’t even get along with each other. Why should I believe?”

Those words stung, and they helped him understand Jesus’ prayer: “that they may be perfected into one, that the world may know that you sent me” (John 17:23). Unity is not interior decoration; it is a witness to the outside world. The world may not read the Bible, but it will read our relationships. The way we treat one another is the window through which the world sees the gospel.

The brother went on to invite co-workers from each camp out for a meal separately. He didn’t rush to judge who was right; he listened, apologized for his own indifference, and asked the pastor to help mediate. Things weren’t resolved overnight, but the tone in the group chat slowly changed. Six months later, his co-worker came to the fellowship’s Christmas gathering. “I wanted to see how you all made peace,” he said. Unity is the most powerful invitation to the gospel.
lessons.light: From an earthly point of view to a heavenly one: unity is not “just taking care of myself” but letting Christ’s love be seen among us. The self-centered person cares only about his own spirituality; the selfless person is willing to pay a price for unity. This is the fulfillment of the year’s core scripture: love one another, so that people recognize us as the Lord’s disciples.
think: In John 17:20-23, what is the purpose of Jesus’ prayer for unity?
Have I ever “chosen silence and minded my own business” in a conflict within a group?
What concrete step could I take toward unity in one of my groups?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for praying for me on the very night you were betrayed. Forgive me for so often caring only about my own spiritual life and standing by while rifts open around me. Make me an instrument of unity in my family, my church, and my group chats, so that the world may recognize from our love for one another that the Father sent you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, pray for a group with a rift in it (your extended family, your fellowship, or a workplace chat), and send a private message to one member you rarely interact with, sincerely asking how they are doing.
lessons.quick: The world may not read the Bible, but it reads our relationships; unity is the most powerful invitation to the gospel.
text: “Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word,
that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.
The glory which you have given me, I have given to them, that they may be one, even as we are one,
I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one, that the world may know that you sent me and loved them, even as you loved me.

lessons.title: In Deed and Truth
lessons.hear:
When John wrote his letters late in life, he condensed everything he had learned into one sentence: “By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (1 John 3:16). Then he puts it very practically: “let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:18). A whole year of lessons must finally land in action.

The 321 Vision has a path—the Way of Service: Spirit · Insight · Life · Serve · God—that helps us walk love out. Spirit: the Holy Spirit is my guide, so I start by praying and asking. Insight: I grasp and obey the truth of Scripture, letting the word correct my motives. Life: I cultivate and live out the life of Jesus, loving through the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit. Serve: I let Jesus reign and serve in his authority and power. God: all glory goes to God, and I give thanks in everything. These five steps are like a staircase, beginning with prayer and ending with thanksgiving.

Today, we will use this path to show love to a real person. Perhaps it is an elderly neighbor who lives alone—you could bring over a meal and sit with them. Perhaps it is a sister in your group chat whose messages are often seen but never answered—you could message her privately to encourage her. Perhaps it is a friend you have long wanted to share the gospel with—you could simply invite him for a meal and listen to how life is going. You don’t have to do something big, but you do have to actually do it.

At the same time, invite people into your “235” group for next year: two or three spiritual companions of the same sex who trust each other, who commit to meeting regularly, reading Scripture together, and praying for one another—each also walking alongside one or two younger believers and serving together on a church team. One person’s zeal will cool, but a group walking together can go the distance. Love means laying down our lives, and it also means small, concrete acts of self-denial every day.
lessons.light: The Way of Service—Spirit · Insight · Life · Serve · God—is the everyday path of letting Jesus reign. Self-centered love stops at words; selfless love steps into action. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. A meal, a message, a visit—each is a footprint of the coming kingdom. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: this is how love walks out the door.
think: In 1 John 3:16-18, how does John define love?
In which relationship does my love often stay “in word only, or with the tongue only”?
Toward which real person will I walk the Way of Service—Spirit · Insight · Life · Serve · God—today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you laid down your life for me, and so I know what love is. Don’t let my love stay on my lips; let it land in my actions. Today I want to walk your Way of Service: first asking the Holy Spirit, obeying your word, living out your life, serving in your strength, and finally giving the glory to you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, show concrete love to a real person: visit a neighbor who lives alone, message an overlooked friend with encouragement, or invite a friend who is exploring the faith to a meal. Also send a message inviting two companions to form a 235 group with you next year.
lessons.quick: Love is not in word or tongue only; walk it out through Spirit · Insight · Life · Serve · God.
text: By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, then closes his heart of compassion against him, how does God’s love remain in him?
My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.

lessons.title: Remember, Repent, Return
lessons.hear:
The end of the year is a time to look back. The risen Lord said to the church in Ephesus, “I know your works, and your toil and perseverance” (Revelation 2:2). The Lord saw their good first, and only then said, gently yet seriously, “But I have this against you, that you left your first love” (Revelation 2:4). Even a hardworking church can forget love in the middle of its busyness.

Let’s use the year’s five-fold change to quietly examine ourselves. Mindset: have I shifted from “Whom do I need?” to “Who needs me?” Life: in which relationships have I seen the fruit of the Spirit, and where am I still bound by self-centeredness? Living: are my words, my phone, and my time more like Christ’s? Relationships: have I repaired a broken friendship or forgiven someone who hurt me? Ministry: have I begun to show hospitality, walk alongside others, and become an ambassador of reconciliation?

You will probably find a great deal of progress, and a great deal still unfinished. That is normal. The Lord’s correction to Ephesus has three steps, as simple as the road home: “Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works” (Revelation 2:5). Remember—recall how moved you were when you first knew the Lord’s love. Repent—admit that you have put service ahead of love. Do the first works—go back to the simple acts of love: praying for people, reaching out first, inviting someone for a meal.

Peter denied the Lord three times, yet the Lord asked him three times, “Do you love me?” and then entrusted his sheep to him. When the Lord reviews us, it is never to eliminate us but to send us out again. So don’t carry guilt into the new year; carry your first love. Love is where every relationship begins, and where it ends.
lessons.light: Among the eight steps of changing a mindset, review and adjustment is not self-condemnation but a return to our first love. Change begins with me: all five aspects of change, from mindset to ministry, must finally come back to a heart filled with the love of Jesus. When we rely on the Spirit with our hearts, we find joy; when we rely on ourselves with our heads, we find worry.
think: In Revelation 2:2-5, what does the Lord affirm first, and what does he rebuke?
Looking back over the five-fold change, what is my greatest growth and what remains most unfinished?
Starting next year, which simple act of love will I take up again as one of the “first works”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for seeing my labor this year, and thank you for gently reminding me of my first love. I confess that I have sometimes put tasks ahead of people and mistaken busyness for love. Help me remember, repent, and do the first works again, carrying your love into the new year. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, spend twenty minutes writing one sentence of year-end review for each area: mindset, life, living, relationships, and ministry. Then write down one simple act of love you will begin again next year, and share it with your companion.
lessons.quick: The Lord reviews us not to eliminate us, but to call us back to our first love.
text: “To the angel of the assembly in Ephesus write: “He who holds the seven stars in his right hand, he who walks among the seven golden lamp stands says these things:
“I know your works, and your toil and perseverance, and that you can’t tolerate evil men, and have tested those who call themselves apostles, and they are not, and found them false.
You have perseverance and have endured for my name’s sake, and have not grown weary.
But I have this against you, that you left your first love.
Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works; or else I am coming to you swiftly, and will move your lamp stand out of its place, unless you repent.

lessons.title: From Every Nation
lessons.hear:
The Bible’s final social picture is a gathering that never ends: “After these things I looked, and behold, a great multitude which no man could count, out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9). People from Taiwan, Malaysia, China, Singapore, and New Zealand; from cities and villages; people who once misunderstood each other, even enemies—all worshiping there with one voice. That is the final completion of all reconciliation.

This picture tells us that every relationship today carries eternal weight. A word of blessing at a class reunion, a visit in your neighborhood, a reconciliation in a group chat—any of these may be where someone’s journey to that throne began. We long and pray for a great revival in the last days: not through the excitement of events, but through millions of ordinary Christians letting Jesus reign in their own networks of relationships. The Lord promises, “Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

Over this year we have moved from mindset to life, from living to relationships, and finally to ministry. Now it is time to be sent. You are sent back into your home as an ambassador of reconciliation; back into your company as salt and light; into your 235 group as a companion, a spiritual parent, and a comrade-in-arms. Our mission is to walk alongside every person until they become an overcomer. The Lord says, “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne” (Revelation 3:21).

So pass on what you have received this year to one person. Perhaps it is a friend who has just come to faith—you could invite him to take this course with you next year. Perhaps it is your child—you could tell, at the dinner table, one story of what God did in your relationships this year. As we wait for the Lord’s return, let us walk alongside one another in love and say together, “Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).
lessons.light: Building God’s system ends in a great chorus before the throne. 920 lets every relationship bear fruit, 235 passes life on from generation to generation, and in the end all glory goes to the One who sits on the throne and to the Lamb. When our focus is on Jesus, we see that today’s small acts of love all lead to eternal glory. This is our sending, and it is our hope.

lessons.speak: God who sits on the throne, and the Lamb: blessing, glory, wisdom, and thanksgiving belong to you. Thank you for walking with me through this year. Now I am willing to be sent by you back into my family, my workplace, and my community as an ambassador of reconciliation, walking alongside each person until they become an overcomer, as I wait for your return. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, recommend or share this course with a friend and tell him one true story of what God did in your relationships this year. Then set the date for your 235 group’s first meeting next year.
lessons.quick: Every small act of love today leads to that never-ending gathering before the throne.
